name: 90/90 Hip Stretch
instructions:
1) Set up on a mat for 90/90 Hip Stretch with a stable base and a neutral-ish pelvis.
2) Move into the stretch or CAP/controlled articulation slowly until you feel a clear but tolerable tissue stretch—not sharp pain.
3) Breathe into the hips; on each exhale, see if a small amount of range appears without forcing.
4) Reverse out carefully and note left–right differences for the next set.
tips:
- Mild stretch is useful; nerve-like zinging is not—back off.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the ribs from flaring just to "get deeper."
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: 90/90 Hip Stretch is a hip-mobility drill that explores controlled range around the hip socket while the pelvis and spine stay relatively organized. Primary emphasis is on hips. Better hip access often makes squats, lunges, and sitting posture feel less stuck. Focus on packed shoulders throughout each rep of 90/90 Hip Stretch.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into the low back → shorten range and re-stack pelvis.
- Holding breath → use slow nasal breaths if possible.
- Forcing the knee with the hands → guide gently; let the hip rotate.
- Rushing side to side → spend quality time on the tighter side.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp groin, pinching, or radiating pain.
- Post-surgery or known labral issues: stay in clinician-approved ranges.
- Warm tissues with easy movement before long end-range holds.

name: Ab Wheel Rollout
instructions:
1) Set up for Ab Wheel Rollout with an ab wheel, finding a neutral ribcage-over-pelvis position before you add challenge.
2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.
tips:
- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Ab Wheel Rollout trains trunk stiffness, anti-movement control, or controlled flexion/rotation depending on the variation—so the spine can transfer force between hips and shoulders. Primary emphasis is on core. A resilient midsection improves lifting positions, running posture, and everyday carrying tasks. Treat Ab Wheel Rollout as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Hips sagging in plank-style work → elevate hands or shorten the hold.
- Yanking with hip flexors on leg raises → posteriorly tilt the pelvis and lead with the lower abs.
- Holding breath until dizzy → use a slow exhale under effort.
- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.
safety_notes:
- Disc-sensitive backs often do better with anti-extension/anti-rotation than aggressive loaded flexion—choose regressions that stay pain-free.
- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Agility Ladder Drills
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Agility Ladder Drills.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.
tips:
- Quality footwork and soft landings matter as much as scoreboard intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Drink water between bouts in long pickup games.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Agility Ladder Drills is sport-skill or game-based conditioning that blends aerobic work with change of direction, timing, and decision-making. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Treat technique and safe spacing as part of the workout—not an afterthought. Treat Agility Ladder Drills as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Going max intensity with cold tissues → warm up first.
- Planting awkwardly on tired legs → shorten sessions when form gets reckless.
- Ignoring rest in continuous games → schedule drink/rest breaks.
- Holding rigid breath under pressure → reset with an exhale between plays.
safety_notes:
- Use appropriate footwear and clear playing space.
- Stop for acute joint injuries; do not "run off" sharp pain.
- Match competitive intensity to your current conditioning and skill.

name: Ankle Alphabet
instructions:
1) Set your foot position for Ankle Alphabet with the heel down when the drill requires it.
2) Move the knee or foot through the prescribed arc slowly, keeping pressure distributed through the foot.
3) Pause in the challenging but non-painful end range and breathe.
4) Return and repeat, matching effort on both sides.
tips:
- Drive the knee toward the little-toe side for many dorsiflexion drills to free the ankle.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the heel heavy when the drill calls for it—cheating the heel up skips the point.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Ankle Alphabet improves ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion control so the knee can travel more freely in squats and lunges. Primary emphasis is on calves. Small daily doses often beat rare aggressive stretching. Keep every rep of Ankle Alphabet looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Pronating hard to fake range → guide the knee more over mid-toes/little toe as coached.
- Bouncing aggressively → use slow oscillations or static holds.
- Ignoring the stiffer side → start sets there.
- Holding breath → exhale into the end range.
safety_notes:
- Sharp Achilles or joint-line pain means stop and regress.
- Recent ankle sprains need gradual, controlled range—not forced stretches.
- Pair mobility with strength in the new range (e.g., heel-elevated squats) when appropriate.

name: Arc Trainer
instructions:
1) Set the machine for Arc Trainer with a stable stance/seat and familiarize yourself with start/stop and resistance controls.
2) Begin easy for 2–3 minutes, then bring intensity to the target zone.
3) Keep posture tall, hands light on rails (unless the machine requires a grip), and movement smooth.
4) Breathe evenly. Cool down by lowering resistance before stepping off carefully.
tips:
- Light fingertip support is fine; hanging on the rails usually means resistance is too high.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use perceived effort or heart-rate zones rather than random max resistance.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Arc Trainer is machine-based cardio that lets you control resistance and pace with predictable mechanics. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. It is useful for aerobic training when outdoor impact needs to stay low or weather limits options. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Arc Trainer.
common_mistakes:
- Over-gripping rails → reduce resistance and stand/ pedal taller.
- Shuffling with collapsed posture → take slightly longer, deliberate strides/strokes.
- Skipping cool-down → spend 2 minutes easy before dismount.
- Holding breath on climbs → exhale on harder segments.
safety_notes:
- Know how to stop the belt/ pedals before you start.
- Step off only after the machine has slowed.
- Stop for dizziness, chest pain, or unusual joint pain.

name: Archer Push-Up
instructions:
1) Set a rigid plank line for Archer Push-Up with hands placed so wrists stack roughly under elbows at the bottom; keep legs long and glutes lightly engaged.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Archer Push-Up is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Archer Push-Up.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Archer Push-Up if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Arnold Press
instructions:
1) Set a stable stance for Arnold Press with the working implement racked at shoulder height, wrists neutral, and ribs down.
2) Brace the trunk, gently tuck the pelvis under so the low back does not dump into extension, and keep the chin slightly tucked.
3) Press the load upward in a smooth path, moving the head slightly back if needed so the arms can finish stacked over the mid-foot.
4) Lock out with biceps by the ears (or as far as mobility allows), then lower under control to the start. Exhale through the press.
tips:
- "Ribs down, glutes on" keeps the press from turning into a backbend.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If wrists bend back hard, lower the load and grip more through the heel of the palm.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Arnold Press is an overhead pressing pattern that builds shoulder and upper-body pressing strength while demanding trunk stability. Primary emphasis is on shoulders. It teaches you to stack force from the ground through a braced torso into the arms. Treat Arnold Press as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Excessive lumbar arch → squeeze glutes and shorten the range until stack improves.
- Pressing forward out in front of the face → finish the bar/bells over mid-foot.
- Flaring ribs every rep → reset brace before each press.
- Shrugging the shoulders to the ears at lockout → reach long through the arms while keeping neck long.
safety_notes:
- Skip heavy overhead work if overhead mobility is blocked—use landmine or incline press regressions.
- Stop for sharp shoulder impingement pain; adjust elbow path or regress.
- Clear the area overhead and use a controlled lockout, not a violent snap.

name: Assault Bike
instructions:
1) Set seat height for Assault Bike so the knee stays soft at the bottom of the stroke (roughly 25–35°), with a stable, comfortable reach to the bars.
2) Start easy for a few minutes, then bring cadence and resistance to the session target.
3) Pedal smoothly—push through the mid-foot and avoid bouncing in the saddle.
4) Keep a tall-ish torso for the bike type you are on and breathe evenly. Cool down with easy spinning.
tips:
- Cadence around 80–100 rpm suits many aerobic rides; strength spins may go slower with more resistance.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If knees track inward, check seat height and gently guide knees forward over the feet.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Assault Bike is cycling-based cardio that loads the legs through a circular pedal stroke with low impact on the joints. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps, with hamstrings and calves assisting for control and finish. It builds aerobic capacity and quad endurance while allowing precise control of resistance and cadence. Focus on packed shoulders throughout each rep of Assault Bike.
common_mistakes:
- Seat too low (knees collapsing) → raise seat gradually.
- Mashing huge gears at tiny cadence → spin faster with moderate resistance.
- Shrugging on the bars → soften elbows and drop shoulders.
- Holding breath on climbs → exhale on hard pedal strokes.
safety_notes:
- Clip-in users should practice unclipping in a safe area first.
- Stop for sharp knee pain—adjust seat or reduce resistance.
- Stay hydrated on longer indoor sessions.

name: Australian Pull-Up
instructions:
1) Grip your bodyweight for Australian Pull-Up with shoulders set down away from the ears and a gentle hollow/brace through the trunk.
2) Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then drive elbows down toward the ribs/pockets.
3) Pull until the chin clears the bar or the handle reaches the target line for this variation, without shrugging into the neck.
4) Lower through a full, controlled reach. Exhale on the pull; keep legs quiet unless the variation uses a kip intentionally.
tips:
- Pack the shoulders before the first pull—start from structure, not a dead hang shrug.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use a band or foot assist before adding swing if you cannot control the eccentric.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Australian Pull-Up is a vertical pulling pattern that trains the lats and upper back to pull the body (or a load) along a high-to-low path. Primary emphasis is on back. It develops climbing strength, shoulder resilience, and torso control in a hang or overhead reach. Keep every rep of Australian Pull-Up looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Chin jutting to "cheat" height → pull the chest toward the bar and keep neck long.
- Half reps at the bottom → earn a full scapular reach each time.
- Excessive swinging → tighten the trunk and slow the lowering phase.
- Elbows flaring wildly → keep elbows tracking more under the wrists.
safety_notes:
- Elbow or shoulder pain on full hangs → shorten range or use an assisted variation.
- Dropping from the top without control overloads the elbows—own the eccentric.
- Warm up shoulders with lighter scap pulls before hard sets of Australian Pull-Up.

name: Back Extension
instructions:
1) Set a stable posture for Back Extension with the working implement, isolating the intended joint while the rest of the body stays quiet.
2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Back Extension is an accessory pattern focused on strengthening a specific muscle group with a controlled joint action. Primary emphasis is on back and core. Used after compound lifts (or on recovery-focused days), it helps shore up weak links without needing maximal systemic fatigue. Keep every rep of Back Extension looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Swinging the weight → shorten range and slow the eccentric.
- Shrugging or leaning to finish reps → fix posture first, then move the joint.
- Rushing the stretch position → own the lengthened end without pain.
- Partial lockouts every set → use a range you can repeat cleanly.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint pain; mild muscle burn is expected, pinching is not.
- Keep wrists neutral on curl/extension patterns when possible.
- Pair isolation work with compounds rather than replacing foundational patterns entirely.

name: Back Squat
instructions:
1) Set your stance for Back Squat with feet roughly shoulder-width (adjust for comfort), toes slightly out, and weight balanced over mid-foot while holding your bodyweight.
2) Brace your trunk as if preparing for a light cough, keep ribs stacked over pelvis, and unlock the hips and knees together to descend.
3) Descend until thighs reach at least parallel (or your reliable pain-free depth), keeping knees tracking over mid-toes without collapsing inward.
4) Drive through the floor to stand, finishing with hips and knees extended without hyperextending the low back. Breathe out through the effort of the ascent.
tips:
- Cue "knees out, chest proud" so the hips stay organized under the torso.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If heels lift, shorten depth or elevate heels slightly until ankle mobility catches up.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Back Squat is a knee-dominant lower-body strength pattern that loads the hips and knees together through a squat stance. Primary emphasis is on glutes and quadriceps. Practiced well, it builds usable leg strength for standing, climbing, and athletic change of direction while teaching you to keep the torso braced over a stable mid-foot balance. Treat Back Squat as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Knees cave inward → gently push knees toward little toes and feel outer glutes.
- Butt wink / pelvis tucking hard at the bottom → raise depth to the last clean position.
- Leaning excessively forward → sit between the heels more and keep mid-foot pressure.
- Cutting the top short → stand tall and squeeze glutes without pushing the hips forward past the ribs.
safety_notes:
- Stop if you feel sharp knee, hip, or spine pain—reduce depth or switch to a supported squat variation.
- Keep heels down; bouncing out of a collapsed bottom position increases joint stress.
- Warm up with bodyweight squats before loading Back Squat.

name: Backstroke Swim
instructions:
1) Enter safely and take a few easy lengths or width crossings to feel the water for Backstroke Swim.
2) Establish horizontal alignment—long spine, light core engagement, head in line with the spine.
3) Stroke with the intended pattern, rotating or kicking as the stroke requires, and breathe without lifting the head excessively.
4) Keep a sustainable pace; rest on the wall as needed. Exit carefully when finished.
tips:
- Relax the neck; gaze slightly downward in freestyle-type postures.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorter, smoother strokes usually beat thrashing when tired.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Backstroke Swim is swim-based conditioning that combines breath control, horizontal posture, and coordinated limb propulsion. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Swimming is joint-friendly cardio when technique stays relaxed and breathing is rhythmic. Focus on packed shoulders throughout each rep of Backstroke Swim.
common_mistakes:
- Holding breath too long → practice bilateral or comfortable rhythmic breathing.
- Crossing the midline with the hands → reach forward in the shoulder line.
- Kicking from bent knees only → initiate kick from the hips with soft knees.
- Tensing traps the whole set → exhale bubbles and soften the shoulders.
safety_notes:
- Swim in supervised areas appropriate to your skill level.
- Stop for dizziness, chest pain, or shoulder impingement that alters the stroke.
- Do not push hard sets without an easy warm-up in the water.

name: Band Dislocate

3) Breathe through the end range without shrugging into the ears.
4) Reverse carefully and compare sides.
tips:
- Think "long neck, heavy shoulder blades" during stretches.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- If you only feel the front of the shoulder pinching, reduce range and adjust angle.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Band Dislocate restores usable motion through the shoulders, thoracic spine, or chest so overhead and pressing postures feel less cramped. Keep every rep of Band Dislocate looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring ribs to reach overhead → re-stack and shorten the reach.
- Shrugging to force range → depress shoulders and move slower.
- Turning a shoulder drill into a low-back stretch → keep pelvis quiet.
- Bouncing into end range → use controlled holds.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp impingement or numbness/tingling down the arm.
- Post-dislocation or post-op shoulders: stay inside approved ranges.
- Warm up before aggressive end-range band work.

- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

- Breath leads; depth follows.

- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.

- Butt wink / pelvis tucking hard at the bottom → raise depth to the last clean position.
- Leaning excessively forward → sit between the heels more and keep mid-foot pressure.
- Cutting the top short → stand tall and squeeze glutes without pushing the hips forward past the ribs.
safety_notes:
- Stop if you feel sharp knee, hip, or spine pain—reduce depth or switch to a supported squat variation.
- Keep heels down; bouncing out of a collapsed bottom position increases joint stress.
- Warm up with bodyweight squats before loading Bulgarian Split Squat.

name: Burpees
instructions:
1) Set an athletic stance for Burpees with your bodyweight if used, weight on mid-foot, and eyes forward.
2) Load the hips and knees quickly (or step into the jump as prescribed), then extend through hips, knees, and ankles to leave the ground.
3) Land softly on the mid-foot with knees tracking over toes and hips absorbing like springs.
4) Reset between reps if quality drops. Breathe out on the effort of the jump.
tips:
- Quiet landings beat maximal height when learning.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Use arms deliberately; floppy arms waste power.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Burpees is a plyometric or rebound-focused pattern that trains elastic power and landing control. Primary emphasis is on glutes and calves, with quadriceps and core assisting for control and finish. Power comes from a crisp takeoff—and from absorbing force quietly on the landing. Keep every rep of Burpees looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Landing with locked knees → soften hips and knees on contact.
- Knees collapsing inward → push knees toward little toes on takeoff and landing.
- Cutting the landing short and rushing → stick the landing for a beat.
- Holding breath → exhale on the jump effort.
safety_notes:
- High-impact volume adds up—limit hard contacts when sore or under-recovered.
- Use an appropriate box height; step down if needed instead of bouncing off.
- Stop for sharp Achilles, knee, or low-back pain.

name: Butterfly Stretch
instructions:
1) Set up on a mat for Butterfly Stretch with a stable base and a neutral-ish pelvis.
2) Move into the stretch or CAP/controlled articulation slowly until you feel a clear but tolerable tissue stretch—not sharp pain.
3) Breathe into the hips; on each exhale, see if a small amount of range appears without forcing.
4) Reverse out carefully and note left–right differences for the next set.
tips:
- Mild stretch is useful; nerve-like zinging is not—back off.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the ribs from flaring just to "get deeper."
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Butterfly Stretch is a hip-mobility drill that explores controlled range around the hip socket while the pelvis and spine stay relatively organized. Primary emphasis is on hips. Better hip access often makes squats, lunges, and sitting posture feel less stuck. Focus on packed shoulders throughout each rep of Butterfly Stretch.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into the low back → shorten range and re-stack pelvis.
- Holding breath → use slow nasal breaths if possible.
- Forcing the knee with the hands → guide gently; let the hip rotate.
- Rushing side to side → spend quality time on the tighter side.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp groin, pinching, or radiating pain.
- Post-surgery or known labral issues: stay in clinician-approved ranges.
- Warm tissues with easy movement before long end-range holds.

name: Cable Chest Fly
instructions:
1) Plant your feet for Cable Chest Fly, grip a cable handle, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Cable Chest Fly is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Cable Chest Fly.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Cable Chest Fly if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Cable Crunch
instructions:
1) Set up for Cable Crunch with a cable handle, finding a neutral ribcage-over-pelvis position before you add challenge.
2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.
tips:
- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Cable Crunch trains trunk stiffness, anti-movement control, or controlled flexion/rotation depending on the variation—so the spine can transfer force between hips and shoulders. Primary emphasis is on core. A resilient midsection improves lifting positions, running posture, and everyday carrying tasks. Focus on smooth eccentrics throughout each rep of Cable Crunch.
common_mistakes:
- Hips sagging in plank-style work → elevate hands or shorten the hold.
- Yanking with hip flexors on leg raises → posteriorly tilt the pelvis and lead with the lower abs.
- Holding breath until dizzy → use a slow exhale under effort.
- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.
safety_notes:
- Disc-sensitive backs often do better with anti-extension/anti-rotation than aggressive loaded flexion—choose regressions that stay pain-free.
- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Cable Curl
instructions:
1) Set a stable posture for Cable Curl with a cable handle, isolating the intended joint while the rest of the body stays quiet.
2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Cable Curl is an accessory pattern focused on strengthening a specific muscle group with a controlled joint action. Primary emphasis is on biceps. Used after compound lifts (or on recovery-focused days), it helps shore up weak links without needing maximal systemic fatigue. Treat Cable Curl as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Swinging the weight → shorten range and slow the eccentric.
- Shrugging or leaning to finish reps → fix posture first, then move the joint.
- Rushing the stretch position → own the lengthened end without pain.
- Partial lockouts every set → use a range you can repeat cleanly.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint pain; mild muscle burn is expected, pinching is not.
- Keep wrists neutral on curl/extension patterns when possible.
- Pair isolation work with compounds rather than replacing foundational patterns entirely.

name: Cable Kick Back

4) Return to the start and reset. Exhale through the hardest portion of the effort.
tips:
- Chase position ownership before chasing load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Film a set occasionally to catch drift you cannot feel.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Cable Kick Back is a strength pattern trained with a cable handle to improve force production and control. Primary emphasis is on glutes. - Rushing setup → reset feet/bracing every set.
- Cutting range when tired → reduce load instead.
- Losing brace mid-rep → shorter sets with cleaner positions.
- Holding a panicked breath → use a braced breathing pattern.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint or spine pain.
- Progress load gradually across weeks.
- Keep the area clear of trip hazards before loaded sets.

name: Cadence Intervals
instructions:
1) Set seat height for Cadence Intervals so the knee stays soft at the bottom of the stroke (roughly 25–35°), with a stable, comfortable reach to the bars.
2) Start easy for a few minutes, then bring cadence and resistance to the session target.
3) Pedal smoothly—push through the mid-foot and avoid bouncing in the saddle.
4) Keep a tall-ish torso for the bike type you are on and breathe evenly. Cool down with easy spinning.
tips:
- Cadence around 80–100 rpm suits many aerobic rides; strength spins may go slower with more resistance.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If knees track inward, check seat height and gently guide knees forward over the feet.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Cadence Intervals is cycling-based cardio that loads the legs through a circular pedal stroke with low impact on the joints. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps, with hamstrings and calves assisting for control and finish. It builds aerobic capacity and quad endurance while allowing precise control of resistance and cadence. Keep every rep of Cadence Intervals looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Seat too low (knees collapsing) → raise seat gradually.
- Mashing huge gears at tiny cadence → spin faster with moderate resistance.
- Shrugging on the bars → soften elbows and drop shoulders.
- Holding breath on climbs → exhale on hard pedal strokes.
safety_notes:
- Clip-in users should practice unclipping in a safe area first.
- Stop for sharp knee pain—adjust seat or reduce resistance.
- Stay hydrated on longer indoor sessions.

name: Calf Stretch On Step
instructions:
1) Set your foot position for Calf Stretch On Step with the heel down when the drill requires it.
2) Move the knee or foot through the prescribed arc slowly, keeping pressure distributed through the foot.
3) Pause in the challenging but non-painful end range and breathe.
4) Return and repeat, matching effort on both sides.
tips:
- Drive the knee toward the little-toe side for many dorsiflexion drills to free the ankle.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the heel heavy when the drill calls for it—cheating the heel up skips the point.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Calf Stretch On Step improves ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion control so the knee can travel more freely in squats and lunges. Primary emphasis is on calves. Small daily doses often beat rare aggressive stretching. Focus on packed shoulders throughout each rep of Calf Stretch On Step.
common_mistakes:
- Pronating hard to fake range → guide the knee more over mid-toes/little toe as coached.
- Bouncing aggressively → use slow oscillations or static holds.
- Ignoring the stiffer side → start sets there.
- Holding breath → exhale into the end range.
safety_notes:
- Sharp Achilles or joint-line pain means stop and regress.
- Recent ankle sprains need gradual, controlled range—not forced stretches.
- Pair mobility with strength in the new range (e.g., heel-elevated squats) when appropriate.

name: Calf Wall Stretch
instructions:
1) Set up for Calf Wall Stretch with a long spine and the working leg positioned as the drill requires.
2) Hinge or extend until you feel a clear hamstring stretch—keep the back from excessively rounding just to go deeper.
3) Breathe and hold or oscillate gently in a tolerable range.
4) Ease out and switch sides.
tips:
- A soft knee often lets you feel hamstrings more than a locked, painful knee.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Pointing the toes up can bias different parts of the posterior chain—explore gently.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Calf Wall Stretch targets hamstring length and tolerance to hip flexion with a relatively extended knee. Primary emphasis is on hamstrings. Useful before hinge work or after long sitting—without forcing a rounded back for extra inches. Treat Calf Wall Stretch as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Rounding hard through the low back → shorten range and lengthen the spine.
- Yanking into deeper ranges → use breath and time under gentle tension.
- Ignoring neurological symptoms → back off if you get sharp shooting pain.
- Holding breath → slow exhales.
safety_notes:
- Sciatica-like symptoms mean stay gentle and consider professional guidance.
- Do not bounce aggressively into end range.
- Pair stretching with hinge strength so new range is usable.

name: Captain's Chair Leg Raise
instructions:
1) Set up for Captain's Chair Leg Raise on the working implement with stable support and an easy starting posture.
2) Move slowly into the target range until you feel a mild-to-moderate stretch or joint challenge without sharp pain.
3) Breathe and own the position; add tiny oscillations only if they stay smooth.
4) Exit carefully and repeat on both sides when relevant.
tips:
- Consistency beats once-a-week extreme stretching.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Pair new range with light strength in that range when possible.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Captain's Chair Leg Raise is a mobility drill that expands usable joint range and tissue tolerance with controlled movement. Primary emphasis is on core. Treat it as practice for positions you want to own in training—not a flexibility contest. Keep every rep of Captain's Chair Leg Raise looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Forcing range with breath held → back off and breathe.
- Compensating with other joints → reduce range until the target joint moves.
- Comparing sides with ego → train the tighter side first.
- Bouncing hard → use controlled tempo.
safety_notes:
- Sharp pain is a stop signal.
- Warm tissues before long end-range holds.
- Seek professional guidance for post-injury mobility plans when needed.

name: Cat Cow Flow
instructions:
1) Set a stable base for Cat Cow Flow on a mat with an easy breath.
2) Initiate the spinal motion from the intended region (neck, mid-back, or low back as prescribed) rather than heaving from one stuck spot.
3) Move through a comfortable arc, matching breath to the motion (often exhale into flexion, inhale into extension—but comfort rules).
4) Return to neutral with control.
tips:
- Small, honest ranges beat dramatic collapsing shapes.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep hips relatively quiet unless the drill includes hip motion.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Cat Cow Flow explores controlled spinal flexion, extension, or rotation to keep the trunk moving segment by segment. Primary emphasis is on back. Move like you are oiling each vertebra—smooth and pain-free beats aggressive end-range forcing. Keep every rep of Cat Cow Flow looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into one hinge point → distribute motion along the spine.
- Holding breath → keep air moving.
- Rushing rotations → move as if balancing a glass on the head.
- Forcing end range with arms → let the torso lead.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp spine pain, dizziness, or neurological symptoms.
- Disc-sensitive individuals may prefer smaller ranges and more support.
- Warm up before deep end-range twisting under load.

- Post-dislocation or post-op shoulders: stay inside approved ranges.

name: Chest Supported Row
instructions:
1) Set your stance or seat for Chest Supported Row with the working implement, arms long, and shoulders packed away from the ears.
2) Brace lightly, initiate by driving the elbows back, and pull the implement toward the ribcage/abdomen as the variation requires.
3) Squeeze the shoulder blades toward the back pockets at the end range without shrugging upward.
4) Return to a full reach with control—keep tension so the shoulders do not dump forward passively.

- Pull with the elbows, not by yanking the wrists.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.

description: Chest Supported Row is a horizontal pulling pattern that strengthens the upper back and scapular retractors while balancing pressing volume. Primary emphasis is on back. Strong rows improve posture under fatigue and help the shoulders tolerate pressing and daily reaching. Focus on full usable range throughout each rep of Chest Supported Row.
common_mistakes:
- Shrugging every rep → depress shoulders and lead with elbows.
- Using momentum from the hips/low back → pause briefly at full reach, then row.
- Cutting the range short → reach long without losing the brace, then pull fully.
- Craning the neck forward → keep eyes roughly forward and neck long.
safety_notes:
- Avoid yanking into end-range if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.
- Keep ribs from flaring on seated variations—brace first.
- Build volume gradually when returning from upper-back fatigue.

name: Child's Pose to Down Dog
instructions:
1) Set a stable base for Child's Pose to Down Dog on a mat with an easy breath.
2) Initiate the spinal motion from the intended region (neck, mid-back, or low back as prescribed) rather than heaving from one stuck spot.
3) Move through a comfortable arc, matching breath to the motion (often exhale into flexion, inhale into extension—but comfort rules).
4) Return to neutral with control.
tips:
- Small, honest ranges beat dramatic collapsing shapes.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep hips relatively quiet unless the drill includes hip motion.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Child's Pose to Down Dog explores controlled spinal flexion, extension, or rotation to keep the trunk moving segment by segment. Primary emphasis is on back. Move like you are oiling each vertebra—smooth and pain-free beats aggressive end-range forcing. Focus on full usable range throughout each rep of Child's Pose to Down Dog.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into one hinge point → distribute motion along the spine.
- Holding breath → keep air moving.
- Rushing rotations → move as if balancing a glass on the head.
- Forcing end range with arms → let the torso lead.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp spine pain, dizziness, or neurological symptoms.
- Disc-sensitive individuals may prefer smaller ranges and more support.
- Warm up before deep end-range twisting under load.

name: Chin Up
instructions:
1) Grip your bodyweight for Chin Up with shoulders set down away from the ears and a gentle hollow/brace through the trunk.
2) Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then drive elbows down toward the ribs/pockets.
3) Pull until the chin clears the bar or the handle reaches the target line for this variation, without shrugging into the neck.
4) Lower through a full, controlled reach. Exhale on the pull; keep legs quiet unless the variation uses a kip intentionally.
tips:
- Pack the shoulders before the first pull—start from structure, not a dead hang shrug.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Use a band or foot assist before adding swing if you cannot control the eccentric.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Chin Up is a vertical pulling pattern that trains the lats and upper back to pull the body (or a load) along a high-to-low path. Primary emphasis is on back. It develops climbing strength, shoulder resilience, and torso control in a hang or overhead reach. Keep every rep of Chin Up looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Chin jutting to "cheat" height → pull the chest toward the bar and keep neck long.
- Half reps at the bottom → earn a full scapular reach each time.
- Excessive swinging → tighten the trunk and slow the lowering phase.
- Elbows flaring wildly → keep elbows tracking more under the wrists.
safety_notes:
- Elbow or shoulder pain on full hangs → shorten range or use an assisted variation.
- Dropping from the top without control overloads the elbows—own the eccentric.
- Warm up shoulders with lighter scap pulls before hard sets of Chin Up.

name: Clapping Push-Up
instructions:
1) Warm up briefly before Clapping Push-Up until breathing and tissues feel ready.
2) Move at the intended intensity with posture you could maintain for the whole bout.
3) Adjust pace if form breaks—quality first.
4) Cool down with easier movement and steady breathing.
tips:
- Use talk-test or RPE to guide intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Consistency beats occasional hero sessions.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

name: ClimbMill
instructions:
1) Set the machine for ClimbMill with a stable stance/seat and familiarize yourself with start/stop and resistance controls.
2) Begin easy for 2–3 minutes, then bring intensity to the target zone.
3) Keep posture tall, hands light on rails (unless the machine requires a grip), and movement smooth.
4) Breathe evenly. Cool down by lowering resistance before stepping off carefully.
tips:
- Light fingertip support is fine; hanging on the rails usually means resistance is too high.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use perceived effort or heart-rate zones rather than random max resistance.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: ClimbMill is machine-based cardio that lets you control resistance and pace with predictable mechanics. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. It is useful for aerobic training when outdoor impact needs to stay low or weather limits options. Focus on quiet landings throughout each rep of ClimbMill.
common_mistakes:
- Over-gripping rails → reduce resistance and stand/ pedal taller.
- Shuffling with collapsed posture → take slightly longer, deliberate strides/strokes.
- Skipping cool-down → spend 2 minutes easy before dismount.
- Holding breath on climbs → exhale on harder segments.
safety_notes:
- Know how to stop the belt/ pedals before you start.
- Step off only after the machine has slowed.
- Stop for dizziness, chest pain, or unusual joint pain.

name: Close Grip Bench Press
instructions:
1) Plant your feet for Close Grip Bench Press, grip the working implement, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- A closer grip shifts more work to triceps—keep elbows tracking, not pinching painfully into the sides.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Close Grip Bench Press is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest and triceps. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Keep every rep of Close Grip Bench Press looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Close Grip Bench Press if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Close Grip Lat Pull Down
instructions:
1) Set your stance and grip for Close Grip Lat Pull Down with a machine, bracing the trunk before the first move.
2) Move through the intended range with even control, keeping joints stacked.
3) Pause briefly in the hardest honest position if it improves ownership.
4) Return to the start and reset. Exhale through the hardest portion of the effort.
tips:
- Chase full usable range without compensation before chasing load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Film a set occasionally to catch drift you cannot feel.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Close Grip Lat Pull Down is a strength pattern trained with a machine to improve force production and control. Primary emphasis is on back. Prioritize a strong setup, smooth tempo, and a finish position you could photograph on every rep. Focus on mid-foot balance throughout each rep of Close Grip Lat Pull Down.
common_mistakes:
- Rushing setup → reset feet/bracing every set.
- Cutting range when tired → reduce load instead.
- Losing brace mid-rep → shorter sets with cleaner positions.
- Holding a panicked breath → use a braced breathing pattern.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint or spine pain.
- Progress load gradually across weeks.
- Keep the area clear of trip hazards before loaded sets.

name: Concentration Curl
instructions:
1) Set a stable posture for Concentration Curl with the working implement, isolating the intended joint while the rest of the body stays quiet.
2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.

name: Conventional Deadlift
instructions:
1) Set up for Conventional Deadlift with the working implement, feet hip-width, and a soft bend in the knees you can hold steady.
2) Brace the trunk, unlock the hips first, and push them rearward while the torso leans as one piece—imagine closing a car door with your hips.
3) Lower until you feel a strong hamstring load or reach the technique depth for this variation, keeping the bar/weight close to the legs if applicable.
4) Drive the floor away and bring hips forward to stand tall. Exhale as the hips finish under the shoulders.
tips:
- Soft knees stay fixed; the motion is hips back, not a deep squat.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Keep the load close to your center of mass—drifting away increases shear on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

common_mistakes:
- Rounding the upper or lower back → shorten the range and re-brace before hinging.
- Squatting the hinge (knees slide forward too much) → push hips back and keep shins more vertical.
- Hyperextending at lockout → finish tall with glutes, not by dumping into the low back.
- Yanking the weight with the arms → let the hips create the power.
safety_notes:
- Avoid max loading if you cannot keep a long, braced spine through the whole set.
- Sharp shooting pain down a leg or into the spine is a stop signal—regress to a shorter hinge.
- Build hinge confidence with lighter loads and slower eccentrics before adding speed.

name: Couch Stretch
instructions:

2) Move into the stretch or CAP/controlled articulation slowly until you feel a clear but tolerable tissue stretch—not sharp pain.

- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.

- Holding breath → use slow nasal breaths if possible.
- Forcing the knee with the hands → guide gently; let the hip rotate.
- Rushing side to side → spend quality time on the tighter side.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp groin, pinching, or radiating pain.
- Post-surgery or known labral issues: stay in clinician-approved ranges.
- Warm tissues with easy movement before long end-range holds.

name: Crab Walk
instructions:

2) Brace the trunk and move through the pattern with even tempo—no collapsing at the hard point.

4) Return to the start under control and reset before the next rep.

- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Neck craning → keep a long neck and soft gaze.
safety_notes:
- Joint pinching means adjust hand/foot placement or range.
- Build volume gradually—bodyweight work can still overload tendons.
- Stop sets when positions deform rather than chasing failure every time.

name: Cricket
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Cricket.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.
tips:
- Quality footwork and soft landings matter as much as scoreboard intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Drink water between bouts in long pickup games.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

safety_notes:

- Stop for acute joint injuries; do not "run off" sharp pain.
- Match competitive intensity to your current conditioning and skill.

name: Cross Body Shoulder Stretch
instructions:
1) Set a stable spine for Cross Body Shoulder Stretch on a mat, lightly braced so the ribs stay down.
2) Explore the shoulder/T-spine path with smooth arcs or holds as prescribed.
3) Breathe through the end range without shrugging into the ears.
4) Reverse carefully and compare sides.

- Think "long neck, heavy shoulder blades" during stretches.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.

- If you only feel the front of the shoulder pinching, reduce range and adjust angle.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

common_mistakes:
- Flaring ribs to reach overhead → re-stack and shorten the reach.
- Shrugging to force range → depress shoulders and move slower.
- Turning a shoulder drill into a low-back stretch → keep pelvis quiet.
- Bouncing into end range → use controlled holds.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp impingement or numbness/tingling down the arm.
- Post-dislocation or post-op shoulders: stay inside approved ranges.
- Warm up before aggressive end-range band work.

name: Crunch
instructions:
1) Set up for Crunch with your bodyweight, finding a neutral ribcage-over-pelvis position before you add challenge.
2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.

- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.

- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Cycling
instructions:
1) Set seat height for Cycling so the knee stays soft at the bottom of the stroke (roughly 25–35°), with a stable, comfortable reach to the bars.
2) Start easy for a few minutes, then bring cadence and resistance to the session target.
3) Pedal smoothly—push through the mid-foot and avoid bouncing in the saddle.
4) Keep a tall-ish torso for the bike type you are on and breathe evenly. Cool down with easy spinning.
tips:
- Cadence around 80–100 rpm suits many aerobic rides; strength spins may go slower with more resistance.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If knees track inward, check seat height and gently guide knees forward over the feet.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Cycling is cycling-based cardio that loads the legs through a circular pedal stroke with low impact on the joints. Focus on mid-foot balance throughout each rep of Cycling.
common_mistakes:
- Seat too low (knees collapsing) → raise seat gradually.
- Mashing huge gears at tiny cadence → spin faster with moderate resistance.
- Shrugging on the bars → soften elbows and drop shoulders.
- Holding breath on climbs → exhale on hard pedal strokes.
safety_notes:
- Clip-in users should practice unclipping in a safe area first.
- Stop for sharp knee pain—adjust seat or reduce resistance.
- Stay hydrated on longer indoor sessions.

name: Damper Cap Row
instructions:
1) Strap feet securely for Damper Cap Row, sit tall, and grab the handle with a relaxed grip.
2) Catch position: shins vertical-ish, arms long, shoulders in front of hips with a flat back.
3) Drive through the legs first, then open the hips, then draw the handle to the lower ribs. Reverse on the recovery: arms, hips, then knees.
4) Breathe out on the drive, in on the recovery. Keep strokes smooth rather than yanking with the arms.
tips:
- Legs do most of the work; arms finish.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Aim for a recovery that is longer than the drive on easy aerobic meters.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Damper Cap Row is a full-body cardio pull that sequences legs–hips–trunk–arms on a rower or similar erg. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Damper Cap Row.
common_mistakes:
- Early arm pull → keep arms long until legs nearly finish.
- Rounding at the catch → hinge with a braced flat back.
- Shooting the seat (legs only, then yank) → connect legs and hips as one drive.
- Over-leaning at the finish → lean slightly, then recover immediately.
safety_notes:
- Lower intensity if you feel sharp low-back pain at the catch.
- Build volume gradually—rowers can spike heart rate quickly.
- Keep the chain/path clear and feet strapped.

name: Dead Bug

- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Pair new range with light strength in that range when possible.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

instructions:

2) Move into the stretch or CAP/controlled articulation slowly until you feel a clear but tolerable tissue stretch—not sharp pain.
3) Breathe into the hips; on each exhale, see if a small amount of range appears without forcing.
4) Reverse out carefully and note left–right differences for the next set.
tips:
- Mild stretch is useful; nerve-like zinging is not—back off.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the ribs from flaring just to "get deeper."
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

common_mistakes:
- Dumping into the low back → shorten range and re-stack pelvis.

- Forcing the knee with the hands → guide gently; let the hip rotate.
- Rushing side to side → spend quality time on the tighter side.

- Stop for sharp groin, pinching, or radiating pain.
- Post-surgery or known labral issues: stay in clinician-approved ranges.
- Warm tissues with easy movement before long end-range holds.

instructions:
1) Plant your feet for Floor Press, grip the working implement, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.

- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.

name: Goblet Squat
instructions:
1) Set your stance for Goblet Squat with feet roughly shoulder-width (adjust for comfort), toes slightly out, and weight balanced over mid-foot while holding your bodyweight.
2) Brace your trunk as if preparing for a light cough, keep ribs stacked over pelvis, and unlock the hips and knees together to descend.
3) Descend until thighs reach at least parallel (or your reliable pain-free depth), keeping knees tracking over mid-toes without collapsing inward.

safety_notes:
- Stop if you feel sharp knee, hip, or spine pain—reduce depth or switch to a supported squat variation.
- Keep heels down; bouncing out of a collapsed bottom position increases joint stress.
- Warm up with bodyweight squats before loading Goblet Squat.

name: Good Morning
instructions:
1) Set up for Good Morning with a barbell, feet hip-width, and a soft bend in the knees you can hold steady.
2) Brace the trunk, unlock the hips first, and push them rearward while the torso leans as one piece—imagine closing a car door with your hips.
3) Lower until you feel a strong hamstring load or reach the technique depth for this variation, keeping the bar/weight close to the legs if applicable.
4) Drive the floor away and bring hips forward to stand tall. Exhale as the hips finish under the shoulders.
tips:
- Soft knees stay fixed; the motion is hips back, not a deep squat.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Keep the load close to your center of mass—drifting away increases shear on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Good Morning is a hip-hinge pattern that loads the posterior chain while the knees stay relatively soft, not deeply bent like a squat. Primary emphasis is on hamstrings. It teaches you to move from the hips with a neutral spine—useful for picking things up, sprint mechanics, and resilient back/hip strength. Treat Good Morning as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Rounding the upper or lower back → shorten the range and re-brace before hinging.
- Squatting the hinge (knees slide forward too much) → push hips back and keep shins more vertical.
- Hyperextending at lockout → finish tall with glutes, not by dumping into the low back.
- Yanking the weight with the arms → let the hips create the power.
safety_notes:
- Avoid max loading if you cannot keep a long, braced spine through the whole set.
- Sharp shooting pain down a leg or into the spine is a stop signal—regress to a shorter hinge.
- Build hinge confidence with lighter loads and slower eccentrics before adding speed.

name: Gripper Squeeze
instructions:
1) Set your stance and grip for Gripper Squeeze with the working implement, bracing the trunk before the first move.
2) Move through the intended range with even control, keeping joints stacked.
3) Pause briefly in the hardest honest position if it improves ownership.
4) Return to the start and reset. Exhale through the hardest portion of the effort.
tips:
- Chase smooth tempo before chasing load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Film a set occasionally to catch drift you cannot feel.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Gripper Squeeze is a strength pattern trained with the working implement to improve force production and control. Primary emphasis is on forearms. Prioritize a strong setup, smooth tempo, and a finish position you could photograph on every rep. Treat Gripper Squeeze as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Rushing setup → reset feet/bracing every set.
- Cutting range when tired → reduce load instead.
- Losing brace mid-rep → shorter sets with cleaner positions.
- Holding a panicked breath → use a braced breathing pattern.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint or spine pain.
- Progress load gradually across weeks.
- Keep the area clear of trip hazards before loaded sets.

name: Hack Squat
instructions:
1) Set your stance for Hack Squat with feet roughly shoulder-width (adjust for comfort), toes slightly out, and weight balanced over mid-foot while holding the machine.
2) Brace your trunk as if preparing for a light cough, keep ribs stacked over pelvis, and unlock the hips and knees together to descend.
3) Descend until thighs reach at least parallel (or your reliable pain-free depth), keeping knees tracking over mid-toes without collapsing inward.
4) Drive through the floor to stand, finishing with hips and knees extended without hyperextending the low back. Breathe out through the effort of the ascent.
tips:
- Cue "knees out, chest proud" so the hips stay organized under the torso.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If heels lift, shorten depth or elevate heels slightly until ankle mobility catches up.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Hack Squat is a knee-dominant lower-body strength pattern that loads the hips and knees together through a squat stance. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps. Practiced well, it builds usable leg strength for standing, climbing, and athletic change of direction while teaching you to keep the torso braced over a stable mid-foot balance. Treat Hack Squat as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Knees cave inward → gently push knees toward little toes and feel outer glutes.
- Butt wink / pelvis tucking hard at the bottom → raise depth to the last clean position.
- Leaning excessively forward → sit between the heels more and keep mid-foot pressure.
- Cutting the top short → stand tall and squeeze glutes without pushing the hips forward past the ribs.
safety_notes:
- Stop if you feel sharp knee, hip, or spine pain—reduce depth or switch to a supported squat variation.
- Keep heels down; bouncing out of a collapsed bottom position increases joint stress.
- Warm up with bodyweight squats before loading Hack Squat.

name: Hammer Curl
instructions:
1) Set a stable posture for Hammer Curl with the working implement, isolating the intended joint while the rest of the body stays quiet.
2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Hammer Curl is an accessory pattern focused on strengthening a specific muscle group with a controlled joint action. Primary emphasis is on biceps. Used after compound lifts (or on recovery-focused days), it helps shore up weak links without needing maximal systemic fatigue. Keep every rep of Hammer Curl looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Swinging the weight → shorten range and slow the eccentric.
- Shrugging or leaning to finish reps → fix posture first, then move the joint.
- Rushing the stretch position → own the lengthened end without pain.
- Partial lockouts every set → use a range you can repeat cleanly.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint pain; mild muscle burn is expected, pinching is not.
- Keep wrists neutral on curl/extension patterns when possible.
- Pair isolation work with compounds rather than replacing foundational patterns entirely.

name: Hamstring Stretch with Yoga Strap
instructions:
1) Arrive on the rings for Hamstring Stretch with Yoga Strap, take a preparatory breath, and set a long spine.
2) Move into the pose piece by piece—feet/hands first, then hips/shoulders, then head gaze.
3) Soften where you can without collapsing the foundation; breathe steadily through the nose if comfortable.
4) Exit with control to a neutral position. Notice the after-effect rather than yanking out of the shape.
tips:
- Breath leads; depth follows.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Micro-bend joints if you tend to lock aggressively.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Hamstring Stretch with Yoga Strap is a yoga-inspired mobility and control posture that links breath with a deliberate shape. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. The aim is a calm, sustainable position—not forcing end range for its own sake. Focus on smooth eccentrics throughout each rep of Hamstring Stretch with Yoga Strap.
common_mistakes:
- Forcing depth with breath held → back out and breathe.
- Collapsing into the shoulders/neck → press the floor away and keep neck long.
- Comparing your shape to photos → use sensation and stability as the guide.
- Bouncing in end range → stay still and breathe.
safety_notes:
- Sharp joint or spine pain means ease out immediately.
- Modify with blocks/bolsters rather than muscling into ranges you do not own.
- Avoid aggressive end-range stretching on cold tissues—warm up first.

name: Handstand Hold
instructions:
1) Set up for Handstand Hold on a stable surface or apparatus with your bodyweight, establishing a braced hollow or stacked posture first.
2) Move into the skill position with control—use a regression entry if you cannot float into the full expression yet.
3) Hold or perform reps while keeping shoulders packed and the trunk quiet; quality beats duration vanity.
4) Exit the position deliberately to a safe finish. Breathe calmly; panic breath usually means the leverage is too hard.
tips:
- Film a side view occasionally to catch sagging hips or flared ribs.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Train wrists/shoulders with prep work before high-skill volume.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Handstand Hold is a skilled bodyweight strength skill that combines joint control, relative strength, and often balance. Primary emphasis is on shoulders. Progress comes from owning easier regressions before adding leverage, range, or freestanding difficulty. Focus on even left–right effort throughout each rep of Handstand Hold.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into the low back for "more height/hold" → shorten leverage and re-hollow.
- Soft elbows when the skill needs lockout → strengthen lockout regressions.
- Rushing entries → pause in the setup every rep.
- Comparing freestanding progress to supported practice too early → earn consistency first.
safety_notes:
- Use mats and spotters for inversion or high-fall-risk skills.
- Wrist pain means reduce volume and add wrist prep—not pushing through sharp pain.
- Fatigue destroys skill positions; stop the set when form collapses.
