name: High Knee
instructions:
1) Warm up briefly before High Knee until breathing and tissues feel ready.
2) Move at the intended intensity with posture you could maintain for the whole bout.
3) Adjust pace if form breaks—quality first.
4) Cool down with easier movement and steady breathing.
tips:
- Use talk-test or RPE to guide intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Consistency beats occasional hero sessions.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: High Knee is a conditioning effort designed to elevate heart rate and improve work capacity. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Keep technique sustainable so aerobic training builds fitness instead of reinforcing sloppy movement. Keep every rep of High Knee looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Starting too hard → ease in for the first minutes.
- Collapsing posture when tired → shorten the bout.
- Skipping warm-up → keep a short ramp.
- Breath holding → keep a rhythm.
safety_notes:
- Stop for chest pain, faintness, or disproportionate distress.
- Progress duration before intensity when returning from time off.
- Hydrate appropriately for longer sessions.

name: High to Low Cable Fly
instructions:
1) Plant your feet for High to Low Cable Fly, grip a cable handle, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: High to Low Cable Fly is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Focus on full usable range throughout each rep of High to Low Cable Fly.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of High to Low Cable Fly if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Hiit Circuit
instructions:
1) Warm up 3–5 minutes easy before Hiit Circuit so joints and breathing are ready.
2) Hit the work interval at a hard-but-repeatable intensity for the planned time or reps.
3) Use the rest interval to recover posture and breathing—walk, easy pedal, or complete rest as prescribed.
4) Repeat for the planned rounds. Cool down with easy movement and longer exhales.
tips:
- Leave one gear in reserve so the last interval still looks like the first.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Track work:rest so you can progress density thoughtfully next session.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Hiit Circuit is an interval-style conditioning bout that alternates harder efforts with recovery to raise cardiovascular fitness efficiently. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. The goal is repeatable quality across intervals—not a single heroic first round followed by collapse. Keep every rep of Hiit Circuit looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Sprinting round one then fading → pace to finish strong.
- Sloppy form under fatigue → regress the movement, not just the ego.
- Skipping warm-up → keep a short ramp even when short on time.
- Holding breath in work bouts → keep a forceful exhale rhythm.
safety_notes:
- If you feel chest pain, faintness, or disproportionate distress, stop and seek care as needed.
- Beginners should start with longer rests and fewer rounds.
- Pair HIIT with easier days; daily max intervals raise injury and burnout risk.

name: Hiking
instructions:
1) Begin Hiking standing tall with a comfortable stride and relaxed shoulders.
2) Walk at the intended briskness, pushing through the big toe and letting the arms swing naturally opposite the legs.
3) Keep ribs stacked and avoid excessive forward hunch as fatigue rises.
4) Breathe through the nose and mouth as needed; finish by easing the pace for 2–3 minutes.
tips:
- Brisk usually means you can talk in sentences but not sing easily.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Add gentle inclines before adding heavy load on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Hiking is low-impact locomotor cardio that raises heart rate while staying joint-friendly. Primary emphasis is on glutes and calves, with core assisting for control and finish. Brisk walking is a foundational conditioning tool and an excellent recovery-day option between harder sessions. Treat Hiking as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Slouching into the phone → take eyes up and open the chest periodically.
- Overstriding downhill → shorten steps and control the descent.
- Tensing the traps the whole time → relax shoulders down.
- Holding breath on hills → sync exhale with effort.
safety_notes:
- Choose stable footwear and visible routes.
- For rucking/load carries, start with light loads and short distances.
- Stop for chest pain, dizziness, or unusual shortness of breath and seek medical care if needed.

name: Hill Sprint
instructions:
1) Start Hill Sprint with an easy walk or light jog to raise temperature and wake up calves/hips.
2) Settle into the target pace with a tall posture, soft forward lean from the ankles, and quick, light foot contacts under the hips.
3) Keep cadence relatively quick; avoid overstriding that heels slam far in front of the body.
4) Breathe rhythmically (for example, a comfortable 2–2 or 3–3 pattern). Finish with a walk to cool down.
tips:
- Easy days should feel conversational unless the session is explicitly a hard interval.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorten stride and increase cadence if you hear loud heel slamming.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Hill Sprint is a running-based cardio bout focused on sustainable gait mechanics and aerobic (or mixed) conditioning. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps and calves, with glutes and core assisting for control and finish. Easy-to-moderate running builds work capacity; faster variations train speed and anaerobic power when recovered well. Focus on quiet landings throughout each rep of Hill Sprint.
common_mistakes:
- Overstriding → land closer under the hips.
- Hunched chest / crossed arms → open the chest and swing arms forward-back.
- Starting too fast → first minutes easier than ego wants.
- Holding breath on hills → exhale deliberately on the effort.
safety_notes:
- Increase weekly running volume gradually; sudden spikes raise injury risk.
- Sharp shin, knee, or Achilles pain is a stop/regress signal—walk or cross-train.
- Use footwear that feels stable for your gait and surface.

name: Hip Cars
instructions:
1) Set up on a mat for Hip Cars with a stable base and a neutral-ish pelvis.
2) Move into the stretch or CAP/controlled articulation slowly until you feel a clear but tolerable tissue stretch—not sharp pain.
3) Breathe into the hips; on each exhale, see if a small amount of range appears without forcing.
4) Reverse out carefully and note left–right differences for the next set.
tips:
- Mild stretch is useful; nerve-like zinging is not—back off.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the ribs from flaring just to "get deeper."
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Hip Cars is a hip-mobility drill that explores controlled range around the hip socket while the pelvis and spine stay relatively organized. Primary emphasis is on hips, with glutes assisting for control and finish. Better hip access often makes squats, lunges, and sitting posture feel less stuck. Focus on full usable range throughout each rep of Hip Cars.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into the low back → shorten range and re-stack pelvis.
- Holding breath → use slow nasal breaths if possible.
- Forcing the knee with the hands → guide gently; let the hip rotate.
- Rushing side to side → spend quality time on the tighter side.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp groin, pinching, or radiating pain.
- Post-surgery or known labral issues: stay in clinician-approved ranges.
- Warm tissues with easy movement before long end-range holds.

name: Hollow Body Hold
instructions:
1) Set up for Hollow Body Hold with your bodyweight, finding a neutral ribcage-over-pelvis position before you add challenge.
2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.
tips:
- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Hollow Body Hold trains trunk stiffness, anti-movement control, or controlled flexion/rotation depending on the variation—so the spine can transfer force between hips and shoulders. Primary emphasis is on core. A resilient midsection improves lifting positions, running posture, and everyday carrying tasks. Keep every rep of Hollow Body Hold looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Hips sagging in plank-style work → elevate hands or shorten the hold.
- Yanking with hip flexors on leg raises → posteriorly tilt the pelvis and lead with the lower abs.
- Holding breath until dizzy → use a slow exhale under effort.
- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.
safety_notes:
- Disc-sensitive backs often do better with anti-extension/anti-rotation than aggressive loaded flexion—choose regressions that stay pain-free.
- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Ice Hockey
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Ice Hockey.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.
tips:
- Quality footwork and soft landings matter as much as scoreboard intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Drink water between bouts in long pickup games.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Treat technique and safe spacing as part of the workout—not an afterthought. common_mistakes:
- Going max intensity with cold tissues → warm up first.
- Planting awkwardly on tired legs → shorten sessions when form gets reckless.
- Ignoring rest in continuous games → schedule drink/rest breaks.
- Holding rigid breath under pressure → reset with an exhale between plays.
safety_notes:

name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
instructions:
1) Plant your feet for Incline Barbell Bench Press, grip a barbell, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) On an incline, keep shoulder blades lightly set and lower toward the upper chest with elbows about 45° from the torso.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Incline Barbell Bench Press is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Keep every rep of Incline Barbell Bench Press looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Use a spotter or safety pins for heavy barbell sets of Incline Barbell Bench Press.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
instructions:

2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

name: Incline Treadmill Walk
instructions:
1) Begin Incline Treadmill Walk standing tall with a comfortable stride and relaxed shoulders.
2) Walk at the intended briskness, pushing through the big toe and letting the arms swing naturally opposite the legs.
3) Keep ribs stacked and avoid excessive forward hunch as fatigue rises.
4) Breathe through the nose and mouth as needed; finish by easing the pace for 2–3 minutes.
tips:
- Brisk usually means you can talk in sentences but not sing easily.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Add gentle inclines before adding heavy load on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Incline Treadmill Walk is low-impact locomotor cardio that raises heart rate while staying joint-friendly. Primary emphasis is on glutes and calves, with core assisting for control and finish. Brisk walking is a foundational conditioning tool and an excellent recovery-day option between harder sessions. Keep every rep of Incline Treadmill Walk looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Slouching into the phone → take eyes up and open the chest periodically.
- Overstriding downhill → shorten steps and control the descent.
- Tensing the traps the whole time → relax shoulders down.
- Holding breath on hills → sync exhale with effort.
safety_notes:
- Choose stable footwear and visible routes.
- For rucking/load carries, start with light loads and short distances.
- Stop for chest pain, dizziness, or unusual shortness of breath and seek medical care if needed.

name: Interval Run
instructions:
1) Start Interval Run with an easy walk or light jog to raise temperature and wake up calves/hips.
2) Settle into the target pace with a tall posture, soft forward lean from the ankles, and quick, light foot contacts under the hips.
3) Keep cadence relatively quick; avoid overstriding that heels slam far in front of the body.
4) Breathe rhythmically (for example, a comfortable 2–2 or 3–3 pattern). Finish with a walk to cool down.
tips:
- Easy days should feel conversational unless the session is explicitly a hard interval.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorten stride and increase cadence if you hear loud heel slamming.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Interval Run is a running-based cardio bout focused on sustainable gait mechanics and aerobic (or mixed) conditioning. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps and calves, with glutes and core assisting for control and finish. Easy-to-moderate running builds work capacity; faster variations train speed and anaerobic power when recovered well. Keep every rep of Interval Run looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Overstriding → land closer under the hips.
- Hunched chest / crossed arms → open the chest and swing arms forward-back.
- Starting too fast → first minutes easier than ego wants.
- Holding breath on hills → exhale deliberately on the effort.
safety_notes:
- Increase weekly running volume gradually; sudden spikes raise injury risk.
- Sharp shin, knee, or Achilles pain is a stop/regress signal—walk or cross-train.
- Use footwear that feels stable for your gait and surface.

name: Inverted Row
instructions:
1) Set your stance or seat for Inverted Row with your bodyweight, arms long, and shoulders packed away from the ears.
2) Brace lightly, initiate by driving the elbows back, and pull the implement toward the ribcage/abdomen as the variation requires.
3) Squeeze the shoulder blades toward the back pockets at the end range without shrugging upward.
4) Return to a full reach with control—keep tension so the shoulders do not dump forward passively.
tips:
- Pull with the elbows, not by yanking the wrists.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Think "chest to the hands" on bodyweight rows; "hands to the ribs" on loaded rows.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Inverted Row is a horizontal pulling pattern that strengthens the upper back and scapular retractors while balancing pressing volume. Primary emphasis is on back. Strong rows improve posture under fatigue and help the shoulders tolerate pressing and daily reaching. Focus on quiet landings throughout each rep of Inverted Row.
common_mistakes:
- Shrugging every rep → depress shoulders and lead with elbows.
- Using momentum from the hips/low back → pause briefly at full reach, then row.
- Cutting the range short → reach long without losing the brace, then pull fully.
- Craning the neck forward → keep eyes roughly forward and neck long.
safety_notes:
- Avoid yanking into end-range if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.
- Keep ribs from flaring on seated variations—brace first.
- Build volume gradually when returning from upper-back fatigue.

name: IT Band Cross-Over Stretch
instructions:
1) Set up for IT Band Cross-Over Stretch with a long spine and the working leg positioned as the drill requires.
2) Hinge or extend until you feel a clear hamstring stretch—keep the back from excessively rounding just to go deeper.
3) Breathe and hold or oscillate gently in a tolerable range.
4) Ease out and switch sides.
tips:
- A soft knee often lets you feel hamstrings more than a locked, painful knee.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Pointing the toes up can bias different parts of the posterior chain—explore gently.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: IT Band Cross-Over Stretch targets hamstring length and tolerance to hip flexion with a relatively extended knee. Primary emphasis is on hamstrings. Useful before hinge work or after long sitting—without forcing a rounded back for extra inches. Keep every rep of IT Band Cross-Over Stretch looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Rounding hard through the low back → shorten range and lengthen the spine.
- Yanking into deeper ranges → use breath and time under gentle tension.
- Ignoring neurological symptoms → back off if you get sharp shooting pain.
- Holding breath → slow exhales.
safety_notes:
- Sciatica-like symptoms mean stay gentle and consider professional guidance.
- Do not bounce aggressively into end range.
- Pair stretching with hinge strength so new range is usable.

name: Jm Press
instructions:
1) Set your stance and grip for Jm Press with the working implement, bracing the trunk before the first move.
2) Move through the intended range with even control, keeping joints stacked.
3) Pause briefly in the hardest honest position if it improves ownership.
4) Return to the start and reset. Exhale through the hardest portion of the effort.
tips:
- Chase quiet, controlled transitions before chasing load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Film a set occasionally to catch drift you cannot feel.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Jm Press is a strength pattern trained with the working implement to improve force production and control. Primary emphasis is on triceps. Prioritize a strong setup, smooth tempo, and a finish position you could photograph on every rep. Keep every rep of Jm Press looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Rushing setup → reset feet/bracing every set.
- Cutting range when tired → reduce load instead.
- Losing brace mid-rep → shorter sets with cleaner positions.
- Holding a panicked breath → use a braced breathing pattern.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint or spine pain.
- Progress load gradually across weeks.
- Keep the area clear of trip hazards before loaded sets.

name: Jump Rope
instructions:
1) Set an athletic stance for Jump Rope with the working implement if used, weight on mid-foot, and eyes forward.
2) Load the hips and knees quickly (or step into the jump as prescribed), then extend through hips, knees, and ankles to leave the ground.
3) Land softly on the mid-foot with knees tracking over toes and hips absorbing like springs.
4) Reset between reps if quality drops. Breathe out on the effort of the jump.
tips:
- Quiet landings beat maximal height when learning.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use arms deliberately; floppy arms waste power.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Jump Rope is a plyometric or rebound-focused pattern that trains elastic power and landing control. Primary emphasis is on glutes and calves, with quadriceps and core assisting for control and finish. Power comes from a crisp takeoff—and from absorbing force quietly on the landing. Treat Jump Rope as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Landing with locked knees → soften hips and knees on contact.
- Knees collapsing inward → push knees toward little toes on takeoff and landing.
- Cutting the landing short and rushing → stick the landing for a beat.
- Holding breath → exhale on the jump effort.
safety_notes:
- High-impact volume adds up—limit hard contacts when sore or under-recovered.
- Use an appropriate box height; step down if needed instead of bouncing off.
- Stop for sharp Achilles, knee, or low-back pain.

name: KB Snatch Intervals
instructions:
1) Warm up 3–5 minutes easy before KB Snatch Intervals so joints and breathing are ready.
2) Hit the work interval at a hard-but-repeatable intensity for the planned time or reps.
3) Use the rest interval to recover posture and breathing—walk, easy pedal, or complete rest as prescribed.
4) Repeat for the planned rounds. Cool down with easy movement and longer exhales.
tips:
- Leave one gear in reserve so the last interval still looks like the first.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Track work:rest so you can progress density thoughtfully next session.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: KB Snatch Intervals is an interval-style conditioning bout that alternates harder efforts with recovery to raise cardiovascular fitness efficiently. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. The goal is repeatable quality across intervals—not a single heroic first round followed by collapse. Treat KB Snatch Intervals as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Sprinting round one then fading → pace to finish strong.
- Sloppy form under fatigue → regress the movement, not just the ego.
- Skipping warm-up → keep a short ramp even when short on time.
- Holding breath in work bouts → keep a forceful exhale rhythm.
safety_notes:
- If you feel chest pain, faintness, or disproportionate distress, stop and seek care as needed.
- Beginners should start with longer rests and fewer rounds.
- Pair HIIT with easier days; daily max intervals raise injury and burnout risk.

name: Kickboard Drill
instructions:
1) Warm up briefly before Kickboard Drill until breathing and tissues feel ready.
2) Move at the intended intensity with posture you could maintain for the whole bout.
3) Adjust pace if form breaks—quality first.
4) Cool down with easier movement and steady breathing.
tips:
- Use talk-test or RPE to guide intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Consistency beats occasional hero sessions.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Kickboard Drill is a conditioning effort designed to elevate heart rate and improve work capacity. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Keep technique sustainable so aerobic training builds fitness instead of reinforcing sloppy movement. Keep every rep of Kickboard Drill looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.

name: Knee Over Toe Rocks
instructions:
1) Set your foot position for Knee Over Toe Rocks with the heel down when the drill requires it.
2) Move the knee or foot through the prescribed arc slowly, keeping pressure distributed through the foot.
3) Pause in the challenging but non-painful end range and breathe.
4) Return and repeat, matching effort on both sides.
tips:
- Drive the knee toward the little-toe side for many dorsiflexion drills to free the ankle.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the heel heavy when the drill calls for it—cheating the heel up skips the point.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Knee Over Toe Rocks improves ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion control so the knee can travel more freely in squats and lunges. Primary emphasis is on calves. Small daily doses often beat rare aggressive stretching. Keep every rep of Knee Over Toe Rocks looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Pronating hard to fake range → guide the knee more over mid-toes/little toe as coached.
- Bouncing aggressively → use slow oscillations or static holds.
- Ignoring the stiffer side → start sets there.
- Holding breath → exhale into the end range.
safety_notes:
- Sharp Achilles or joint-line pain means stop and regress.
- Recent ankle sprains need gradual, controlled range—not forced stretches.
- Pair mobility with strength in the new range (e.g., heel-elevated squats) when appropriate.

name: Knee-to-Chest Stretch
instructions:
1) Set a stable base for Knee-to-Chest Stretch on a mat with an easy breath.
2) Initiate the spinal motion from the intended region (neck, mid-back, or low back as prescribed) rather than heaving from one stuck spot.
3) Move through a comfortable arc, matching breath to the motion (often exhale into flexion, inhale into extension—but comfort rules).
4) Return to neutral with control.
tips:
- Small, honest ranges beat dramatic collapsing shapes.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep hips relatively quiet unless the drill includes hip motion.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Knee-to-Chest Stretch explores controlled spinal flexion, extension, or rotation to keep the trunk moving segment by segment. Primary emphasis is on back. Move like you are oiling each vertebra—smooth and pain-free beats aggressive end-range forcing. Keep every rep of Knee-to-Chest Stretch looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into one hinge point → distribute motion along the spine.
- Holding breath → keep air moving.
- Rushing rotations → move as if balancing a glass on the head.
- Forcing end range with arms → let the torso lead.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp spine pain, dizziness, or neurological symptoms.
- Disc-sensitive individuals may prefer smaller ranges and more support.
- Warm up before deep end-range twisting under load.

name: L-Sit
instructions:
1) Set up for L-Sit with your bodyweight, finding a neutral ribcage-over-pelvis position before you add challenge.
2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.
tips:
- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: L-Sit trains trunk stiffness, anti-movement control, or controlled flexion/rotation depending on the variation—so the spine can transfer force between hips and shoulders. Primary emphasis is on core. A resilient midsection improves lifting positions, running posture, and everyday carrying tasks. Treat L-Sit as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Hips sagging in plank-style work → elevate hands or shorten the hold.
- Yanking with hip flexors on leg raises → posteriorly tilt the pelvis and lead with the lower abs.
- Holding breath until dizzy → use a slow exhale under effort.
- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.
safety_notes:
- Disc-sensitive backs often do better with anti-extension/anti-rotation than aggressive loaded flexion—choose regressions that stay pain-free.
- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Landmine Press
instructions:
1) Set a stable stance for Landmine Press with the working implement racked at shoulder height, wrists neutral, and ribs down.
2) Brace the trunk, gently tuck the pelvis under so the low back does not dump into extension, and keep the chin slightly tucked.
3) Press the load upward in a smooth path, moving the head slightly back if needed so the arms can finish stacked over the mid-foot.
4) Lock out with biceps by the ears (or as far as mobility allows), then lower under control to the start. Exhale through the press.
tips:
- "Ribs down, glutes on" keeps the press from turning into a backbend.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If wrists bend back hard, lower the load and grip more through the heel of the palm.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Landmine Press is an overhead pressing pattern that builds shoulder and upper-body pressing strength while demanding trunk stability. Primary emphasis is on chest. It teaches you to stack force from the ground through a braced torso into the arms. Treat Landmine Press as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Excessive lumbar arch → squeeze glutes and shorten the range until stack improves.
- Pressing forward out in front of the face → finish the bar/bells over mid-foot.
- Flaring ribs every rep → reset brace before each press.
- Shrugging the shoulders to the ears at lockout → reach long through the arms while keeping neck long.
safety_notes:
- Skip heavy overhead work if overhead mobility is blocked—use landmine or incline press regressions.
- Stop for sharp shoulder impingement pain; adjust elbow path or regress.
- Clear the area overhead and use a controlled lockout, not a violent snap.

name: Lat Pulldown
instructions:
1) Grip a machine for Lat Pulldown with shoulders set down away from the ears and a gentle hollow/brace through the trunk.
2) Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then drive elbows down toward the ribs/pockets.
3) Pull until the chin clears the bar or the handle reaches the target line for this variation, without shrugging into the neck.
4) Lower through a full, controlled reach. Exhale on the pull; keep legs quiet unless the variation uses a kip intentionally.
tips:
- Pack the shoulders before the first pull—start from structure, not a dead hang shrug.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use a band or foot assist before adding swing if you cannot control the eccentric.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Lat Pulldown is a vertical pulling pattern that trains the lats and upper back to pull the body (or a load) along a high-to-low path. Primary emphasis is on back. It develops climbing strength, shoulder resilience, and torso control in a hang or overhead reach. Treat Lat Pulldown as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Chin jutting to "cheat" height → pull the chest toward the bar and keep neck long.
- Half reps at the bottom → earn a full scapular reach each time.
- Excessive swinging → tighten the trunk and slow the lowering phase.
- Elbows flaring wildly → keep elbows tracking more under the wrists.
safety_notes:
- Elbow or shoulder pain on full hangs → shorten range or use an assisted variation.
- Dropping from the top without control overloads the elbows—own the eccentric.
- Warm up shoulders with lighter scap pulls before hard sets of Lat Pulldown.

name: Lateral Bounds
instructions:
1) Warm up briefly before Lateral Bounds until breathing and tissues feel ready.
2) Move at the intended intensity with posture you could maintain for the whole bout.
3) Adjust pace if form breaks—quality first.
4) Cool down with easier movement and steady breathing.
tips:
- Use talk-test or RPE to guide intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Consistency beats occasional hero sessions.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Lateral Bounds is a conditioning effort designed to elevate heart rate and improve work capacity. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Keep technique sustainable so aerobic training builds fitness instead of reinforcing sloppy movement. Focus on quiet landings throughout each rep of Lateral Bounds.
common_mistakes:
- Starting too hard → ease in for the first minutes.
- Collapsing posture when tired → shorten the bout.
- Skipping warm-up → keep a short ramp.
- Breath holding → keep a rhythm.
safety_notes:
- Stop for chest pain, faintness, or disproportionate distress.
- Progress duration before intensity when returning from time off.
- Hydrate appropriately for longer sessions.

name: Lateral Raise
instructions:
1) Set a stable posture for Lateral Raise with the working implement, isolating the intended joint while the rest of the body stays quiet.
2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Lateral Raise is an accessory pattern focused on strengthening a specific muscle group with a controlled joint action. Primary emphasis is on shoulders. Used after compound lifts (or on recovery-focused days), it helps shore up weak links without needing maximal systemic fatigue. Keep every rep of Lateral Raise looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Swinging the weight → shorten range and slow the eccentric.
- Shrugging or leaning to finish reps → fix posture first, then move the joint.
- Rushing the stretch position → own the lengthened end without pain.
- Partial lockouts every set → use a range you can repeat cleanly.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint pain; mild muscle burn is expected, pinching is not.
- Keep wrists neutral on curl/extension patterns when possible.
- Pair isolation work with compounds rather than replacing foundational patterns entirely.

name: Leg Press
instructions:
1) Set your stance for Leg Press with feet roughly shoulder-width (adjust for comfort), toes slightly out, and weight balanced over mid-foot while holding the machine.
2) Brace your trunk as if preparing for a light cough, keep ribs stacked over pelvis, and unlock the hips and knees together to descend.
3) Descend until thighs reach at least parallel (or your reliable pain-free depth), keeping knees tracking over mid-toes without collapsing inward.
4) Drive through the floor to stand, finishing with hips and knees extended without hyperextending the low back. Breathe out through the effort of the ascent.
tips:
- Cue "knees out, chest proud" so the hips stay organized under the torso.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If heels lift, shorten depth or elevate heels slightly until ankle mobility catches up.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Leg Press is a knee-dominant lower-body strength pattern that loads the hips and knees together through a squat stance. Primary emphasis is on glutes and quadriceps. Practiced well, it builds usable leg strength for standing, climbing, and athletic change of direction while teaching you to keep the torso braced over a stable mid-foot balance. Treat Leg Press as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Knees cave inward → gently push knees toward little toes and feel outer glutes.
- Butt wink / pelvis tucking hard at the bottom → raise depth to the last clean position.
- Leaning excessively forward → sit between the heels more and keep mid-foot pressure.
- Cutting the top short → stand tall and squeeze glutes without pushing the hips forward past the ribs.
safety_notes:
- Stop if you feel sharp knee, hip, or spine pain—reduce depth or switch to a supported squat variation.
- Keep heels down; bouncing out of a collapsed bottom position increases joint stress.
- Warm up with bodyweight squats before loading Leg Press.

name: Low Lunge Yoga
instructions:
1) Arrive on a mat for Low Lunge Yoga, take a preparatory breath, and set a long spine.
2) Move into the pose piece by piece—feet/hands first, then hips/shoulders, then head gaze.
3) Soften where you can without collapsing the foundation; breathe steadily through the nose if comfortable.
4) Exit with control to a neutral position. Notice the after-effect rather than yanking out of the shape.
tips:
- Breath leads; depth follows.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Micro-bend joints if you tend to lock aggressively.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Low Lunge Yoga is a yoga-inspired mobility and control posture that links breath with a deliberate shape. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. The aim is a calm, sustainable position—not forcing end range for its own sake. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Low Lunge Yoga.
common_mistakes:
- Forcing depth with breath held → back out and breathe.
- Collapsing into the shoulders/neck → press the floor away and keep neck long.
- Comparing your shape to photos → use sensation and stability as the guide.
- Bouncing in end range → stay still and breathe.
safety_notes:
- Sharp joint or spine pain means ease out immediately.
- Modify with blocks/bolsters rather than muscling into ranges you do not own.
- Avoid aggressive end-range stretching on cold tissues—warm up first.

name: Low to High Cable Fly
instructions:
1) Plant your feet for Low to High Cable Fly, grip a cable handle, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Low to High Cable Fly is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Treat Low to High Cable Fly as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Low to High Cable Fly if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Lying Twist Hold
instructions:
1) Set a stable base for Lying Twist Hold on a mat with an easy breath.
2) Initiate the spinal motion from the intended region (neck, mid-back, or low back as prescribed) rather than heaving from one stuck spot.
3) Move through a comfortable arc, matching breath to the motion (often exhale into flexion, inhale into extension—but comfort rules).
4) Return to neutral with control.
tips:
- Small, honest ranges beat dramatic collapsing shapes.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep hips relatively quiet unless the drill includes hip motion.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Lying Twist Hold explores controlled spinal flexion, extension, or rotation to keep the trunk moving segment by segment. Primary emphasis is on back, with core assisting for control and finish. Move like you are oiling each vertebra—smooth and pain-free beats aggressive end-range forcing. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Lying Twist Hold.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into one hinge point → distribute motion along the spine.
- Holding breath → keep air moving.
- Rushing rotations → move as if balancing a glass on the head.
- Forcing end range with arms → let the torso lead.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp spine pain, dizziness, or neurological symptoms.
- Disc-sensitive individuals may prefer smaller ranges and more support.
- Warm up before deep end-range twisting under load.

name: Machine Row
instructions:
1) Set your stance or seat for Machine Row with the machine, arms long, and shoulders packed away from the ears.
2) Brace lightly, initiate by driving the elbows back, and pull the implement toward the ribcage/abdomen as the variation requires.
3) Squeeze the shoulder blades toward the back pockets at the end range without shrugging upward.
4) Return to a full reach with control—keep tension so the shoulders do not dump forward passively.
tips:
- Pull with the elbows, not by yanking the wrists.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Think "chest to the hands" on bodyweight rows; "hands to the ribs" on loaded rows.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Machine Row is a horizontal pulling pattern that strengthens the upper back and scapular retractors while balancing pressing volume. Primary emphasis is on back. Strong rows improve posture under fatigue and help the shoulders tolerate pressing and daily reaching. Focus on quiet landings throughout each rep of Machine Row.
common_mistakes:
- Shrugging every rep → depress shoulders and lead with elbows.
- Using momentum from the hips/low back → pause briefly at full reach, then row.
- Cutting the range short → reach long without losing the brace, then pull fully.
- Craning the neck forward → keep eyes roughly forward and neck long.
safety_notes:
- Avoid yanking into end-range if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.
- Keep ribs from flaring on seated variations—brace first.
- Build volume gradually when returning from upper-back fatigue.

name: Martial Arts Sparring
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Martial Arts Sparring.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.
tips:
- Quality footwork and soft landings matter as much as scoreboard intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Drink water between bouts in long pickup games.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Martial Arts Sparring is sport-skill or game-based conditioning that blends aerobic work with change of direction, timing, and decision-making. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Treat technique and safe spacing as part of the workout—not an afterthought. Keep every rep of Martial Arts Sparring looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Going max intensity with cold tissues → warm up first.
- Planting awkwardly on tired legs → shorten sessions when form gets reckless.
- Ignoring rest in continuous games → schedule drink/rest breaks.
- Holding rigid breath under pressure → reset with an exhale between plays.
safety_notes:
- Use appropriate footwear and clear playing space.
- Stop for acute joint injuries; do not "run off" sharp pain.
- Match competitive intensity to your current conditioning and skill.

name: Mixed Row Pyramid
instructions:
1) Strap feet securely for Mixed Row Pyramid, sit tall, and grab the handle with a relaxed grip.
2) Catch position: shins vertical-ish, arms long, shoulders in front of hips with a flat back.
3) Drive through the legs first, then open the hips, then draw the handle to the lower ribs. Reverse on the recovery: arms, hips, then knees.
4) Breathe out on the drive, in on the recovery. Keep strokes smooth rather than yanking with the arms.
tips:
- Legs do most of the work; arms finish.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Aim for a recovery that is longer than the drive on easy aerobic meters.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Mixed Row Pyramid is a full-body cardio pull that sequences legs–hips–trunk–arms on a rower or similar erg. Primary emphasis is on back and legs, with core and arms assisting for control and finish. Done well, it trains aerobic power without impact while reinforcing a strong hinge and posture. Focus on packed shoulders throughout each rep of Mixed Row Pyramid.
common_mistakes:
- Early arm pull → keep arms long until legs nearly finish.
- Rounding at the catch → hinge with a braced flat back.
- Shooting the seat (legs only, then yank) → connect legs and hips as one drive.
- Over-leaning at the finish → lean slightly, then recover immediately.
safety_notes:
- Lower intensity if you feel sharp low-back pain at the catch.
- Build volume gradually—rowers can spike heart rate quickly.
- Keep the chain/path clear and feet strapped.

name: Mountain Climber
instructions:
1) Set the machine for Mountain Climber with a stable stance/seat and familiarize yourself with start/stop and resistance controls.
2) Begin easy for 2–3 minutes, then bring intensity to the target zone.
3) Keep posture tall, hands light on rails (unless the machine requires a grip), and movement smooth.
4) Breathe evenly. Cool down by lowering resistance before stepping off carefully.
tips:
- Light fingertip support is fine; hanging on the rails usually means resistance is too high.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use perceived effort or heart-rate zones rather than random max resistance.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Mountain Climber is machine-based cardio that lets you control resistance and pace with predictable mechanics. Primary emphasis is on core. It is useful for aerobic training when outdoor impact needs to stay low or weather limits options. Keep every rep of Mountain Climber looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Over-gripping rails → reduce resistance and stand/ pedal taller.
- Shuffling with collapsed posture → take slightly longer, deliberate strides/strokes.
- Skipping cool-down → spend 2 minutes easy before dismount.
- Holding breath on climbs → exhale on harder segments.
safety_notes:
- Know how to stop the belt/ pedals before you start.
- Step off only after the machine has slowed.
- Stop for dizziness, chest pain, or unusual joint pain.

name: Neck Side Stretch
instructions:
1) Set up for Neck Side Stretch on a mat with stable support and an easy starting posture.
2) Move slowly into the target range until you feel a mild-to-moderate stretch or joint challenge without sharp pain.
3) Breathe and own the position; add tiny oscillations only if they stay smooth.
4) Exit carefully and repeat on both sides when relevant.
tips:
- Consistency beats once-a-week extreme stretching.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Pair new range with light strength in that range when possible.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

- Compensating with other joints → reduce range until the target joint moves.

- Bouncing hard → use controlled tempo.
safety_notes:
- Sharp pain is a stop signal.
- Warm tissues before long end-range holds.
- Seek professional guidance for post-injury mobility plans when needed.

name: Nordic Hamstring Curl

name: Open Book Stretch

name: Open Water Swim
instructions:

- Relax the neck; gaze slightly downward in freestyle-type postures.

name: Outdoor Bike Hill
instructions:
1) Set seat height for Outdoor Bike Hill so the knee stays soft at the bottom of the stroke (roughly 25–35°), with a stable, comfortable reach to the bars.
2) Start easy for a few minutes, then bring cadence and resistance to the session target.
3) Pedal smoothly—push through the mid-foot and avoid bouncing in the saddle.
4) Keep a tall-ish torso for the bike type you are on and breathe evenly. Cool down with easy spinning.
tips:
- Cadence around 80–100 rpm suits many aerobic rides; strength spins may go slower with more resistance.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If knees track inward, check seat height and gently guide knees forward over the feet.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Shrugging on the bars → soften elbows and drop shoulders.

safety_notes:
- Clip-in users should practice unclipping in a safe area first.
- Stop for sharp knee pain—adjust seat or reduce resistance.
- Stay hydrated on longer indoor sessions.

2) Brace the trunk, gently tuck the pelvis under so the low back does not dump into extension, and keep the chin slightly tucked.
3) Press the load upward in a smooth path, moving the head slightly back if needed so the arms can finish stacked over the mid-foot.
4) Lock out with biceps by the ears (or as far as mobility allows), then lower under control to the start. Exhale through the press.
tips:
- "Ribs down, glutes on" keeps the press from turning into a backbend.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If wrists bend back hard, lower the load and grip more through the heel of the palm.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Excessive lumbar arch → squeeze glutes and shorten the range until stack improves.
- Pressing forward out in front of the face → finish the bar/bells over mid-foot.
- Flaring ribs every rep → reset brace before each press.
- Shrugging the shoulders to the ears at lockout → reach long through the arms while keeping neck long.
safety_notes:
- Skip heavy overhead work if overhead mobility is blocked—use landmine or incline press regressions.
- Stop for sharp shoulder impingement pain; adjust elbow path or regress.
- Clear the area overhead and use a controlled lockout, not a violent snap.

instructions:

2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.
tips:
- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Pallof Press trains trunk stiffness, anti-movement control, or controlled flexion/rotation depending on the variation—so the spine can transfer force between hips and shoulders. Primary emphasis is on core. A resilient midsection improves lifting positions, running posture, and everyday carrying tasks. Focus on mid-foot balance throughout each rep of Pallof Press.
common_mistakes:
- Hips sagging in plank-style work → elevate hands or shorten the hold.
- Yanking with hip flexors on leg raises → posteriorly tilt the pelvis and lead with the lower abs.
- Holding breath until dizzy → use a slow exhale under effort.
- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.
safety_notes:
- Disc-sensitive backs often do better with anti-extension/anti-rotation than aggressive loaded flexion—choose regressions that stay pain-free.
- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Pec Deck Fly
instructions:

3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.

- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.

- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Pec Deck Fly if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

tips:
- Mild stretch is useful; nerve-like zinging is not—back off.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the ribs from flaring just to "get deeper."

name: Pistol Squat
instructions:
1) Set your stance for Pistol Squat with feet roughly shoulder-width (adjust for comfort), toes slightly out, and weight balanced over mid-foot while holding your bodyweight.
2) Brace your trunk as if preparing for a light cough, keep ribs stacked over pelvis, and unlock the hips and knees together to descend.
3) On the working side, sit the hip back and down while the knee tracks over the mid-toes; keep the torso tall enough that the heel stays planted.
4) Drive through the floor to stand, finishing with hips and knees extended without hyperextending the low back. Breathe out through the effort of the ascent.
tips:
- Cue "knees out, chest proud" so the hips stay organized under the torso.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- If heels lift, shorten depth or elevate heels slightly until ankle mobility catches up.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Pistol Squat is a knee-dominant lower-body strength pattern that loads the hips and knees together through a squat stance. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps. - Butt wink / pelvis tucking hard at the bottom → raise depth to the last clean position.

name: Plate Pinches
instructions:

4) Return to the start and reset. Exhale through the hardest portion of the effort.
tips:
- Chase smooth tempo before chasing load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Film a set occasionally to catch drift you cannot feel.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Plate Pinches is a strength pattern trained with the working implement to improve force production and control. Primary emphasis is on forearms. - Cutting range when tired → reduce load instead.
- Losing brace mid-rep → shorter sets with cleaner positions.

safety_notes:

- Progress load gradually across weeks.

name: Power Walk
instructions:

name: Preacher Curl
instructions:

- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

name: Prone Press Up
instructions:
1) Set a stable base for Prone Press Up on a mat with an easy breath.
2) Initiate the spinal motion from the intended region (neck, mid-back, or low back as prescribed) rather than heaving from one stuck spot.
3) Move through a comfortable arc, matching breath to the motion (often exhale into flexion, inhale into extension—but comfort rules).
4) Return to neutral with control.
tips:
- Small, honest ranges beat dramatic collapsing shapes.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep hips relatively quiet unless the drill includes hip motion.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Prone Press Up explores controlled spinal flexion, extension, or rotation to keep the trunk moving segment by segment. Primary emphasis is on back. - Dumping into one hinge point → distribute motion along the spine.
- Holding breath → keep air moving.
- Rushing rotations → move as if balancing a glass on the head.

safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp spine pain, dizziness, or neurological symptoms.
- Disc-sensitive individuals may prefer smaller ranges and more support.
- Warm up before deep end-range twisting under load.

name: Pseudo Planche Lean
instructions:
1) Set up for Pseudo Planche Lean on a stable surface or apparatus with your bodyweight, establishing a braced hollow or stacked posture first.
2) Move into the skill position with control—use a regression entry if you cannot float into the full expression yet.
3) Hold or perform reps while keeping shoulders packed and the trunk quiet; quality beats duration vanity.
4) Exit the position deliberately to a safe finish. Breathe calmly; panic breath usually means the leverage is too hard.
tips:
- Film a side view occasionally to catch sagging hips or flared ribs.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Train wrists/shoulders with prep work before high-skill volume.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Pseudo Planche Lean is a skilled bodyweight strength skill that combines joint control, relative strength, and often balance. Primary emphasis is on shoulders. - Dumping into the low back for "more height/hold" → shorten leverage and re-hollow.
- Soft elbows when the skill needs lockout → strengthen lockout regressions.

safety_notes:
- Use mats and spotters for inversion or high-fall-risk skills.
- Wrist pain means reduce volume and add wrist prep—not pushing through sharp pain.
- Fatigue destroys skill positions; stop the set when form collapses.

name: Pull Buoy Swim
instructions:
1) Enter safely and take a few easy lengths or width crossings to feel the water for Pull Buoy Swim.
2) Establish horizontal alignment—long spine, light core engagement, head in line with the spine.
3) Stroke with the intended pattern, rotating or kicking as the stroke requires, and breathe without lifting the head excessively.
4) Keep a sustainable pace; rest on the wall as needed. Exit carefully when finished.
tips:
- Relax the neck; gaze slightly downward in freestyle-type postures.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorter, smoother strokes usually beat thrashing when tired.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Holding breath too long → practice bilateral or comfortable rhythmic breathing.
- Crossing the midline with the hands → reach forward in the shoulder line.

- Swim in supervised areas appropriate to your skill level.
- Stop for dizziness, chest pain, or shoulder impingement that alters the stroke.

name: Pull Up
instructions:

2) Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then drive elbows down toward the ribs/pockets.
3) Pull until the chin clears the bar or the handle reaches the target line for this variation, without shrugging into the neck.
4) Lower through a full, controlled reach. Exhale on the pull; keep legs quiet unless the variation uses a kip intentionally.

- Pack the shoulders before the first pull—start from structure, not a dead hang shrug.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Use a band or foot assist before adding swing if you cannot control the eccentric.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Pull Up is a vertical pulling pattern that trains the lats and upper back to pull the body (or a load) along a high-to-low path. Primary emphasis is on back. It develops climbing strength, shoulder resilience, and torso control in a hang or overhead reach. Keep every rep of Pull Up looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Chin jutting to "cheat" height → pull the chest toward the bar and keep neck long.
- Half reps at the bottom → earn a full scapular reach each time.
- Excessive swinging → tighten the trunk and slow the lowering phase.
- Elbows flaring wildly → keep elbows tracking more under the wrists.

- Elbow or shoulder pain on full hangs → shorten range or use an assisted variation.
- Dropping from the top without control overloads the elbows—own the eccentric.

name: Push Press
instructions:
1) Set a stable stance for Push Press with the working implement racked at shoulder height, wrists neutral, and ribs down.

3) Press the load upward in a smooth path, moving the head slightly back if needed so the arms can finish stacked over the mid-foot.
4) Lock out with biceps by the ears (or as far as mobility allows), then lower under control to the start. Exhale through the press.
tips:
- "Ribs down, glutes on" keeps the press from turning into a backbend.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If wrists bend back hard, lower the load and grip more through the heel of the palm.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Push Press is an overhead pressing pattern that builds shoulder and upper-body pressing strength while demanding trunk stability. Primary emphasis is on shoulders. It teaches you to stack force from the ground through a braced torso into the arms. Keep every rep of Push Press looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Excessive lumbar arch → squeeze glutes and shorten the range until stack improves.
- Pressing forward out in front of the face → finish the bar/bells over mid-foot.
- Flaring ribs every rep → reset brace before each press.
- Shrugging the shoulders to the ears at lockout → reach long through the arms while keeping neck long.
safety_notes:
- Skip heavy overhead work if overhead mobility is blocked—use landmine or incline press regressions.
- Stop for sharp shoulder impingement pain; adjust elbow path or regress.
- Clear the area overhead and use a controlled lockout, not a violent snap.

name: Push-Up
instructions:
1) Set a rigid plank line for Push-Up with hands placed so wrists stack roughly under elbows at the bottom; keep legs long and glutes lightly engaged.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Push-Up is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Treat Push-Up as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Push-Up if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Quad Couch Stretch
instructions:

2) Move into the stretch or CAP/controlled articulation slowly until you feel a clear but tolerable tissue stretch—not sharp pain.

4) Reverse out carefully and note left–right differences for the next set.
tips:
- Mild stretch is useful; nerve-like zinging is not—back off.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the ribs from flaring just to "get deeper."
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Quad Couch Stretch is a hip-mobility drill that explores controlled range around the hip socket while the pelvis and spine stay relatively organized. Primary emphasis is on hamstrings. common_mistakes:
- Dumping into the low back → shorten range and re-stack pelvis.
- Holding breath → use slow nasal breaths if possible.
- Forcing the knee with the hands → guide gently; let the hip rotate.
- Rushing side to side → spend quality time on the tighter side.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp groin, pinching, or radiating pain.
- Post-surgery or known labral issues: stay in clinician-approved ranges.
- Warm tissues with easy movement before long end-range holds.

name: Reverse Lunge
instructions:
1) Start tall with your bodyweight, ribs stacked, and feet ready for the split stance used in Reverse Lunge.
2) Step or set into the lunge/split position with the front foot flat and the back heel lifted as the variation requires.
3) Lower with control until the back knee approaches the floor (or your comfortable depth) while the front knee tracks over the mid-toes.
4) Push through the front mid-foot to return. Keep the pelvis fairly level—avoid collapsing toward the working hip.
tips:
- Think "tall torso, quiet hips" rather than lunging with a floppy trunk.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
