- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Reverse Pec Deck if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Reverse-Grip Triceps Pushdown
instructions:
1) Set a stable posture for Reverse-Grip Triceps Pushdown with the working implement, isolating the intended joint while the rest of the body stays quiet.
2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Reverse-Grip Triceps Pushdown is an accessory pattern focused on strengthening a specific muscle group with a controlled joint action. Primary emphasis is on triceps. Used after compound lifts (or on recovery-focused days), it helps shore up weak links without needing maximal systemic fatigue. Focus on smooth eccentrics throughout each rep of Reverse-Grip Triceps Pushdown.
common_mistakes:
- Swinging the weight → shorten range and slow the eccentric.
- Shrugging or leaning to finish reps → fix posture first, then move the joint.
- Rushing the stretch position → own the lengthened end without pain.
- Partial lockouts every set → use a range you can repeat cleanly.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint pain; mild muscle burn is expected, pinching is not.
- Keep wrists neutral on curl/extension patterns when possible.
- Pair isolation work with compounds rather than replacing foundational patterns entirely.

name: Ring Dip
instructions:
1) Plant your feet for Ring Dip, grip the rings, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Ring Dip is a horizontal pushing pattern that trains the chest, shoulders, and triceps to move a load away from the torso. Primary emphasis is on chest. Strong horizontal pressing supports pressing strength in daily tasks and balances heavy pulling volume. Treat Ring Dip as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring elbows aggressively → bring elbows closer to ~45° and feel the chest/triceps share the load.
- Ribs flaring / low-back arching for leverage → shorten range and re-brace.
- Partial lockouts every rep → finish with control without snapping elbows.
- Bouncing off the chest → pause lightly and press from muscle, not rebound.
safety_notes:
- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.
- Regress to an incline or knee variation of Ring Dip if you cannot control the full range.
- Warm up with lighter sets or easier leverage before hard working sets.

name: Ring Row
instructions:
1) Set your stance or seat for Ring Row with the rings, arms long, and shoulders packed away from the ears.
2) Brace lightly, initiate by driving the elbows back, and pull the implement toward the ribcage/abdomen as the variation requires.
3) Squeeze the shoulder blades toward the back pockets at the end range without shrugging upward.
4) Return to a full reach with control—keep tension so the shoulders do not dump forward passively.
tips:
- Pull with the elbows, not by yanking the wrists.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- Think "chest to the hands" on bodyweight rows; "hands to the ribs" on loaded rows.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Ring Row is a horizontal pulling pattern that strengthens the upper back and scapular retractors while balancing pressing volume. Primary emphasis is on back. Strong rows improve posture under fatigue and help the shoulders tolerate pressing and daily reaching. Treat Ring Row as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Shrugging every rep → depress shoulders and lead with elbows.
- Using momentum from the hips/low back → pause briefly at full reach, then row.
- Cutting the range short → reach long without losing the brace, then pull fully.
- Craning the neck forward → keep eyes roughly forward and neck long.
safety_notes:
- Avoid yanking into end-range if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.
- Keep ribs from flaring on seated variations—brace first.
- Build volume gradually when returning from upper-back fatigue.

name: Romanian Deadlift
instructions:
1) Set up for Romanian Deadlift with the working implement, feet hip-width, and a soft bend in the knees you can hold steady.
2) Brace the trunk, unlock the hips first, and push them rearward while the torso leans as one piece—imagine closing a car door with your hips.
3) Lower until you feel a strong hamstring load or reach the technique depth for this variation, keeping the bar/weight close to the legs if applicable.
4) Drive the floor away and bring hips forward to stand tall. Exhale as the hips finish under the shoulders.
tips:
- Soft knees stay fixed; the motion is hips back, not a deep squat.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Keep the load close to your center of mass—drifting away increases shear on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Romanian Deadlift is a hip-hinge pattern that loads the posterior chain while the knees stay relatively soft, not deeply bent like a squat. Primary emphasis is on back, glutes, and hamstrings. It teaches you to move from the hips with a neutral spine—useful for picking things up, sprint mechanics, and resilient back/hip strength. Keep every rep of Romanian Deadlift looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Rounding the upper or lower back → shorten the range and re-brace before hinging.
- Squatting the hinge (knees slide forward too much) → push hips back and keep shins more vertical.
- Hyperextending at lockout → finish tall with glutes, not by dumping into the low back.
- Yanking the weight with the arms → let the hips create the power.
safety_notes:
- Avoid max loading if you cannot keep a long, braced spine through the whole set.
- Sharp shooting pain down a leg or into the spine is a stop signal—regress to a shorter hinge.
- Build hinge confidence with lighter loads and slower eccentrics before adding speed.

name: Rope Crunch
instructions:
1) Set up for Rope Crunch with a cable, finding a neutral ribcage-over-pelvis position before you add challenge.
2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.
tips:
- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Rope Crunch trains trunk stiffness, anti-movement control, or controlled flexion/rotation depending on the variation—so the spine can transfer force between hips and shoulders. Primary emphasis is on core. A resilient midsection improves lifting positions, running posture, and everyday carrying tasks. Treat Rope Crunch as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Hips sagging in plank-style work → elevate hands or shorten the hold.
- Yanking with hip flexors on leg raises → posteriorly tilt the pelvis and lead with the lower abs.
- Holding breath until dizzy → use a slow exhale under effort.
- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.
safety_notes:
- Disc-sensitive backs often do better with anti-extension/anti-rotation than aggressive loaded flexion—choose regressions that stay pain-free.
- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Rope Pushdown
instructions:
1) Set your stance and grip for Rope Pushdown with the working implement, bracing the trunk before the first move.
2) Move through the intended range with even control, keeping joints stacked.
3) Pause briefly in the hardest honest position if it improves ownership.
4) Return to the start and reset. Exhale through the hardest portion of the effort.
tips:
- Chase bracing before you move before chasing load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Film a set occasionally to catch drift you cannot feel.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Rope Pushdown is a strength pattern trained with the working implement to improve force production and control. Primary emphasis is on triceps. Prioritize a strong setup, smooth tempo, and a finish position you could photograph on every rep. Treat Rope Pushdown as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Rushing setup → reset feet/bracing every set.
- Cutting range when tired → reduce load instead.
- Losing brace mid-rep → shorter sets with cleaner positions.
- Holding a panicked breath → use a braced breathing pattern.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint or spine pain.
- Progress load gradually across weeks.
- Keep the area clear of trip hazards before loaded sets.

name: Row Intervals
instructions:
1) Strap feet securely for Row Intervals, sit tall, and grab the handle with a relaxed grip.
2) Catch position: shins vertical-ish, arms long, shoulders in front of hips with a flat back.
3) Drive through the legs first, then open the hips, then draw the handle to the lower ribs. Reverse on the recovery: arms, hips, then knees.
4) Breathe out on the drive, in on the recovery. Keep strokes smooth rather than yanking with the arms.
tips:
- Legs do most of the work; arms finish.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Aim for a recovery that is longer than the drive on easy aerobic meters.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Row Intervals is a full-body cardio pull that sequences legs–hips–trunk–arms on a rower or similar erg. Primary emphasis is on back and legs, with core and arms assisting for control and finish. Done well, it trains aerobic power without impact while reinforcing a strong hinge and posture. Treat Row Intervals as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Early arm pull → keep arms long until legs nearly finish.
- Rounding at the catch → hinge with a braced flat back.
- Shooting the seat (legs only, then yank) → connect legs and hips as one drive.
- Over-leaning at the finish → lean slightly, then recover immediately.
safety_notes:
- Lower intensity if you feel sharp low-back pain at the catch.
- Build volume gradually—rowers can spike heart rate quickly.
- Keep the chain/path clear and feet strapped.

name: Ruck Walk
instructions:
1) Begin Ruck Walk standing tall with a comfortable stride and relaxed shoulders.
2) Walk at the intended briskness, pushing through the big toe and letting the arms swing naturally opposite the legs.
3) Keep ribs stacked and avoid excessive forward hunch as fatigue rises.
4) Breathe through the nose and mouth as needed; finish by easing the pace for 2–3 minutes.
tips:
- Brisk usually means you can talk in sentences but not sing easily.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Add gentle inclines before adding heavy load on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Ruck Walk is low-impact locomotor cardio that raises heart rate while staying joint-friendly. Primary emphasis is on glutes and calves, with core assisting for control and finish. Brisk walking is a foundational conditioning tool and an excellent recovery-day option between harder sessions. Focus on quiet landings throughout each rep of Ruck Walk.
common_mistakes:
- Slouching into the phone → take eyes up and open the chest periodically.
- Overstriding downhill → shorten steps and control the descent.
- Tensing the traps the whole time → relax shoulders down.
- Holding breath on hills → sync exhale with effort.
safety_notes:
- Choose stable footwear and visible routes.
- For rucking/load carries, start with light loads and short distances.
- Stop for chest pain, dizziness, or unusual shortness of breath and seek medical care if needed.

name: Running
instructions:
1) Start Running with an easy walk or light jog to raise temperature and wake up calves/hips.
2) Settle into the target pace with a tall posture, soft forward lean from the ankles, and quick, light foot contacts under the hips.
3) Keep cadence relatively quick; avoid overstriding that heels slam far in front of the body.
4) Breathe rhythmically (for example, a comfortable 2–2 or 3–3 pattern). Finish with a walk to cool down.
tips:
- Easy days should feel conversational unless the session is explicitly a hard interval.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorten stride and increase cadence if you hear loud heel slamming.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Running is a running-based cardio bout focused on sustainable gait mechanics and aerobic (or mixed) conditioning. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps and calves, with glutes and core assisting for control and finish. Easy-to-moderate running builds work capacity; faster variations train speed and anaerobic power when recovered well. Focus on full usable range throughout each rep of Running.
common_mistakes:
- Overstriding → land closer under the hips.
- Hunched chest / crossed arms → open the chest and swing arms forward-back.
- Starting too fast → first minutes easier than ego wants.
- Holding breath on hills → exhale deliberately on the effort.
safety_notes:
- Increase weekly running volume gradually; sudden spikes raise injury risk.
- Sharp shin, knee, or Achilles pain is a stop/regress signal—walk or cross-train.
- Use footwear that feels stable for your gait and surface.

name: Savasana Breath
instructions:
1) Arrive on a mat for Savasana Breath, take a preparatory breath, and set a long spine.
2) Move into the pose piece by piece—feet/hands first, then hips/shoulders, then head gaze.
3) Soften where you can without collapsing the foundation; breathe steadily through the nose if comfortable.
4) Exit with control to a neutral position. Notice the after-effect rather than yanking out of the shape.
tips:
- Breath leads; depth follows.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Micro-bend joints if you tend to lock aggressively.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Savasana Breath is a yoga-inspired mobility and control posture that links breath with a deliberate shape. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. The aim is a calm, sustainable position—not forcing end range for its own sake. Focus on packed shoulders throughout each rep of Savasana Breath.
common_mistakes:
- Forcing depth with breath held → back out and breathe.
- Collapsing into the shoulders/neck → press the floor away and keep neck long.
- Comparing your shape to photos → use sensation and stability as the guide.
- Bouncing in end range → stay still and breathe.
safety_notes:
- Sharp joint or spine pain means ease out immediately.
- Modify with blocks/bolsters rather than muscling into ranges you do not own.
- Avoid aggressive end-range stretching on cold tissues—warm up first.

name: Scapular Cars
instructions:
1) Set a stable spine for Scapular Cars on a mat, lightly braced so the ribs stay down.
2) Explore the shoulder/T-spine path with smooth arcs or holds as prescribed.
3) Breathe through the end range without shrugging into the ears.
4) Reverse carefully and compare sides.
tips:
- Think "long neck, heavy shoulder blades" during stretches.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- If you only feel the front of the shoulder pinching, reduce range and adjust angle.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Scapular Cars restores usable motion through the shoulders, thoracic spine, or chest so overhead and pressing postures feel less cramped. Primary emphasis is on shoulders and chest, with upper back assisting for control and finish. Move slowly and keep ribs from flaring as a fake substitute for true shoulder range. Treat Scapular Cars as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring ribs to reach overhead → re-stack and shorten the reach.
- Shrugging to force range → depress shoulders and move slower.
- Turning a shoulder drill into a low-back stretch → keep pelvis quiet.
- Bouncing into end range → use controlled holds.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp impingement or numbness/tingling down the arm.
- Post-dislocation or post-op shoulders: stay inside approved ranges.
- Warm up before aggressive end-range band work.

name: Seated Butterfly Hold
instructions:
1) Set up on a mat for Seated Butterfly Hold with a stable base and a neutral-ish pelvis.
2) Move into the stretch or CAP/controlled articulation slowly until you feel a clear but tolerable tissue stretch—not sharp pain.
3) Breathe into the hips; on each exhale, see if a small amount of range appears without forcing.
4) Reverse out carefully and note left–right differences for the next set.
tips:
- Mild stretch is useful; nerve-like zinging is not—back off.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the ribs from flaring just to "get deeper."
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Seated Butterfly Hold is a hip-mobility drill that explores controlled range around the hip socket while the pelvis and spine stay relatively organized. Primary emphasis is on hips, with glutes assisting for control and finish. Better hip access often makes squats, lunges, and sitting posture feel less stuck. Keep every rep of Seated Butterfly Hold looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into the low back → shorten range and re-stack pelvis.
- Holding breath → use slow nasal breaths if possible.
- Forcing the knee with the hands → guide gently; let the hip rotate.
- Rushing side to side → spend quality time on the tighter side.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp groin, pinching, or radiating pain.
- Post-surgery or known labral issues: stay in clinician-approved ranges.
- Warm tissues with easy movement before long end-range holds.

name: Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press
instructions:
1) Set a stable stance for Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press with dumbbells racked at shoulder height, wrists neutral, and ribs down.
2) Brace the trunk, gently tuck the pelvis under so the low back does not dump into extension, and keep the chin slightly tucked.
3) Press the load upward in a smooth path, moving the head slightly back if needed so the arms can finish stacked over the mid-foot.
4) Lock out with biceps by the ears (or as far as mobility allows), then lower under control to the start. Exhale through the press.
tips:
- "Ribs down, glutes on" keeps the press from turning into a backbend.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If wrists bend back hard, lower the load and grip more through the heel of the palm.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press is an overhead pressing pattern that builds shoulder and upper-body pressing strength while demanding trunk stability. Primary emphasis is on shoulders. It teaches you to stack force from the ground through a braced torso into the arms. Focus on smooth eccentrics throughout each rep of Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press.
common_mistakes:
- Excessive lumbar arch → squeeze glutes and shorten the range until stack improves.
- Pressing forward out in front of the face → finish the bar/bells over mid-foot.
- Flaring ribs every rep → reset brace before each press.
- Shrugging the shoulders to the ears at lockout → reach long through the arms while keeping neck long.
safety_notes:
- Skip heavy overhead work if overhead mobility is blocked—use landmine or incline press regressions.
- Stop for sharp shoulder impingement pain; adjust elbow path or regress.
- Clear the area overhead and use a controlled lockout, not a violent snap.

name: Seated Elliptical
instructions:
1) Set the machine for Seated Elliptical with a stable stance/seat and familiarize yourself with start/stop and resistance controls.
2) Begin easy for 2–3 minutes, then bring intensity to the target zone.
3) Keep posture tall, hands light on rails (unless the machine requires a grip), and movement smooth.
4) Breathe evenly. Cool down by lowering resistance before stepping off carefully.
tips:
- Light fingertip support is fine; hanging on the rails usually means resistance is too high.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use perceived effort or heart-rate zones rather than random max resistance.

name: Seated Hamstring Stretch
instructions:

- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

name: Seated Plantar Flex Stretch
instructions:

3) Pause in the challenging but non-painful end range and breathe.
4) Return and repeat, matching effort on both sides.
tips:
- Drive the knee toward the little-toe side for many dorsiflexion drills to free the ankle.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the heel heavy when the drill calls for it—cheating the heel up skips the point.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

name: Seated Spinal Twist
instructions:
1) Set a stable base for Seated Spinal Twist on a mat with an easy breath.
2) Initiate the spinal motion from the intended region (neck, mid-back, or low back as prescribed) rather than heaving from one stuck spot.
3) Move through a comfortable arc, matching breath to the motion (often exhale into flexion, inhale into extension—but comfort rules).
4) Return to neutral with control.
tips:
- Small, honest ranges beat dramatic collapsing shapes.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep hips relatively quiet unless the drill includes hip motion.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Seated Spinal Twist explores controlled spinal flexion, extension, or rotation to keep the trunk moving segment by segment. Primary emphasis is on back. Move like you are oiling each vertebra—smooth and pain-free beats aggressive end-range forcing. Keep every rep of Seated Spinal Twist looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into one hinge point → distribute motion along the spine.
- Holding breath → keep air moving.
- Rushing rotations → move as if balancing a glass on the head.
- Forcing end range with arms → let the torso lead.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp spine pain, dizziness, or neurological symptoms.

- Warm up before deep end-range twisting under load.

name: Shadow Boxing
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Shadow Boxing.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.
tips:
- Quality footwork and soft landings matter as much as scoreboard intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Drink water between bouts in long pickup games.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Treat technique and safe spacing as part of the workout—not an afterthought. common_mistakes:
- Going max intensity with cold tissues → warm up first.
- Planting awkwardly on tired legs → shorten sessions when form gets reckless.
- Ignoring rest in continuous games → schedule drink/rest breaks.
- Holding rigid breath under pressure → reset with an exhale between plays.
safety_notes:
- Use appropriate footwear and clear playing space.
- Stop for acute joint injuries; do not "run off" sharp pain.
- Match competitive intensity to your current conditioning and skill.

name: Shoulder Capsule Stretch
instructions:
1) Set a stable spine for Shoulder Capsule Stretch on a mat, lightly braced so the ribs stay down.
2) Explore the shoulder/T-spine path with smooth arcs or holds as prescribed.
3) Breathe through the end range without shrugging into the ears.
4) Reverse carefully and compare sides.
tips:
- Think "long neck, heavy shoulder blades" during stretches.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- If you only feel the front of the shoulder pinching, reduce range and adjust angle.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Shoulder Capsule Stretch restores usable motion through the shoulders, thoracic spine, or chest so overhead and pressing postures feel less cramped. Primary emphasis is on shoulders and chest, with upper back assisting for control and finish. Move slowly and keep ribs from flaring as a fake substitute for true shoulder range. Focus on mid-foot balance throughout each rep of Shoulder Capsule Stretch.
common_mistakes:
- Flaring ribs to reach overhead → re-stack and shorten the reach.
- Shrugging to force range → depress shoulders and move slower.
- Turning a shoulder drill into a low-back stretch → keep pelvis quiet.
- Bouncing into end range → use controlled holds.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp impingement or numbness/tingling down the arm.
- Post-dislocation or post-op shoulders: stay inside approved ranges.
- Warm up before aggressive end-range band work.

name: Shrimp Squat
instructions:
1) Set your stance for Shrimp Squat with feet roughly shoulder-width (adjust for comfort), toes slightly out, and weight balanced over mid-foot while holding your bodyweight.
2) Brace your trunk as if preparing for a light cough, keep ribs stacked over pelvis, and unlock the hips and knees together to descend.
3) Descend until thighs reach at least parallel (or your reliable pain-free depth), keeping knees tracking over mid-toes without collapsing inward.
4) Drive through the floor to stand, finishing with hips and knees extended without hyperextending the low back. Breathe out through the effort of the ascent.
tips:
- Cue "knees out, chest proud" so the hips stay organized under the torso.
- Drop to a supported or partial-range variation if form breaks.
- Progress with slower eccentrics, longer pauses, or denser sets—not just more weight.
- If heels lift, shorten depth or elevate heels slightly until ankle mobility catches up.
- Only add load or complexity when you can own the full range with crisp control.
description: Shrimp Squat is a knee-dominant lower-body strength pattern that loads the hips and knees together through a squat stance. Primary emphasis is on quadriceps. Practiced well, it builds usable leg strength for standing, climbing, and athletic change of direction while teaching you to keep the torso braced over a stable mid-foot balance. Treat Shrimp Squat as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Knees cave inward → gently push knees toward little toes and feel outer glutes.
- Butt wink / pelvis tucking hard at the bottom → raise depth to the last clean position.
- Leaning excessively forward → sit between the heels more and keep mid-foot pressure.
- Cutting the top short → stand tall and squeeze glutes without pushing the hips forward past the ribs.
safety_notes:
- Stop if you feel sharp knee, hip, or spine pain—reduce depth or switch to a supported squat variation.
- Keep heels down; bouncing out of a collapsed bottom position increases joint stress.
- Warm up with bodyweight squats before loading Shrimp Squat.

name: Side Plank
instructions:
1) Set up for Side Plank with your bodyweight, finding a neutral ribcage-over-pelvis position before you add challenge.
2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.
tips:
- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Side Plank trains trunk stiffness, anti-movement control, or controlled flexion/rotation depending on the variation—so the spine can transfer force between hips and shoulders. Primary emphasis is on core. A resilient midsection improves lifting positions, running posture, and everyday carrying tasks. Keep every rep of Side Plank looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Hips sagging in plank-style work → elevate hands or shorten the hold.
- Yanking with hip flexors on leg raises → posteriorly tilt the pelvis and lead with the lower abs.
- Holding breath until dizzy → use a slow exhale under effort.
- Turning every core drill into a neck strain → keep neck long and eyes soft.
safety_notes:
- Disc-sensitive backs often do better with anti-extension/anti-rotation than aggressive loaded flexion—choose regressions that stay pain-free.
- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Single Arm Cable Row
instructions:
1) Set your stance or seat for Single Arm Cable Row with a cable handle, arms long, and shoulders packed away from the ears.
2) Brace lightly, initiate by driving the elbows back, and pull the implement toward the ribcage/abdomen as the variation requires.
3) Squeeze the shoulder blades toward the back pockets at the end range without shrugging upward.
4) Return to a full reach with control—keep tension so the shoulders do not dump forward passively.
tips:
- Pull with the elbows, not by yanking the wrists.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Think "chest to the hands" on bodyweight rows; "hands to the ribs" on loaded rows.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Single Arm Cable Row is a horizontal pulling pattern that strengthens the upper back and scapular retractors while balancing pressing volume. Primary emphasis is on back. Strong rows improve posture under fatigue and help the shoulders tolerate pressing and daily reaching. Keep every rep of Single Arm Cable Row looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Shrugging every rep → depress shoulders and lead with elbows.
- Using momentum from the hips/low back → pause briefly at full reach, then row.
- Cutting the range short → reach long without losing the brace, then pull fully.
- Craning the neck forward → keep eyes roughly forward and neck long.
safety_notes:
- Avoid yanking into end-range if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.
- Keep ribs from flaring on seated variations—brace first.
- Build volume gradually when returning from upper-back fatigue.

2) Brace the trunk and move through the pattern with even tempo—no collapsing at the hard point.
3) Reach the target depth or lockout for this variation while keeping joints stacked.
4) Return to the start under control and reset before the next rep.
tips:
- Focus on smooth tempo before adding advanced variations.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Elevate hands or shorten range when you cannot control the hardest angle.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Sagging hips or flared ribs → reset brace and shorten the lever.
- Partial reps that avoid the hard range → use a smaller clean range rather than bouncing.

- Neck craning → keep a long neck and soft gaze.
safety_notes:

name: Single Leg Romanian Deadlift
instructions:
1) Set up for Single Leg Romanian Deadlift with the working implement, feet hip-width, and a soft bend in the knees you can hold steady.
2) Brace the trunk, unlock the hips first, and push them rearward while the torso leans as one piece—imagine closing a car door with your hips.
3) Lower until you feel a strong hamstring load or reach the technique depth for this variation, keeping the bar/weight close to the legs if applicable.
4) Drive the floor away and bring hips forward to stand tall. Exhale as the hips finish under the shoulders.
tips:
- Soft knees stay fixed; the motion is hips back, not a deep squat.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Keep the load close to your center of mass—drifting away increases shear on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Single Leg Romanian Deadlift is a hip-hinge pattern that loads the posterior chain while the knees stay relatively soft, not deeply bent like a squat. Primary emphasis is on glutes and hamstrings. It teaches you to move from the hips with a neutral spine—useful for picking things up, sprint mechanics, and resilient back/hip strength. Keep every rep of Single Leg Romanian Deadlift looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.

- Rounding the upper or lower back → shorten the range and re-brace before hinging.
- Squatting the hinge (knees slide forward too much) → push hips back and keep shins more vertical.
- Hyperextending at lockout → finish tall with glutes, not by dumping into the low back.
- Yanking the weight with the arms → let the hips create the power.
safety_notes:
- Avoid max loading if you cannot keep a long, braced spine through the whole set.
- Sharp shooting pain down a leg or into the spine is a stop signal—regress to a shorter hinge.
- Build hinge confidence with lighter loads and slower eccentrics before adding speed.

name: Skater Jump
instructions:
1) Set an athletic stance for Skater Jump with your bodyweight if used, weight on mid-foot, and eyes forward.
2) Load the hips and knees quickly (or step into the jump as prescribed), then extend through hips, knees, and ankles to leave the ground.
3) Land softly on the mid-foot with knees tracking over toes and hips absorbing like springs.
4) Reset between reps if quality drops. Breathe out on the effort of the jump.
tips:
- Quiet landings beat maximal height when learning.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use arms deliberately; floppy arms waste power.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Skater Jump is a plyometric or rebound-focused pattern that trains elastic power and landing control. - Landing with locked knees → soften hips and knees on contact.
- Knees collapsing inward → push knees toward little toes on takeoff and landing.
- Cutting the landing short and rushing → stick the landing for a beat.

safety_notes:
- High-impact volume adds up—limit hard contacts when sore or under-recovered.
- Use an appropriate box height; step down if needed instead of bouncing off.
- Stop for sharp Achilles, knee, or low-back pain.

name: Skierg
instructions:
1) Strap feet securely for Skierg, sit tall, and grab the handle with a relaxed grip.
2) Catch position: shins vertical-ish, arms long, shoulders in front of hips with a flat back.
3) Drive through the legs first, then open the hips, then draw the handle to the lower ribs. Reverse on the recovery: arms, hips, then knees.
4) Breathe out on the drive, in on the recovery. Keep strokes smooth rather than yanking with the arms.
tips:
- Legs do most of the work; arms finish.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Aim for a recovery that is longer than the drive on easy aerobic meters.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Skierg is a full-body cardio pull that sequences legs–hips–trunk–arms on a rower or similar erg. Primary emphasis is on back and legs, with core and arms assisting for control and finish. Done well, it trains aerobic power without impact while reinforcing a strong hinge and posture. Keep every rep of Skierg looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Early arm pull → keep arms long until legs nearly finish.
- Rounding at the catch → hinge with a braced flat back.
- Shooting the seat (legs only, then yank) → connect legs and hips as one drive.
- Over-leaning at the finish → lean slightly, then recover immediately.
safety_notes:
- Lower intensity if you feel sharp low-back pain at the catch.
- Build volume gradually—rowers can spike heart rate quickly.
- Keep the chain/path clear and feet strapped.

name: Skull Crusher

- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

name: Smith Machine Bench Press
instructions:
1) Plant your feet for Smith Machine Bench Press, grip the machine, and set the shoulder blades on a stable base with wrists stacked roughly under elbows at the bottom.
2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.

- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.

- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Shoulder pinching in the bottom is a cue to reduce depth or widen/narrow the grip slightly.

name: Smith Machine Squat
instructions:
1) Set your stance for Smith Machine Squat with feet roughly shoulder-width (adjust for comfort), toes slightly out, and weight balanced over mid-foot while holding the machine.
2) Brace your trunk as if preparing for a light cough, keep ribs stacked over pelvis, and unlock the hips and knees together to descend.
3) Descend until thighs reach at least parallel (or your reliable pain-free depth), keeping knees tracking over mid-toes without collapsing inward.
4) Drive through the floor to stand, finishing with hips and knees extended without hyperextending the low back. Breathe out through the effort of the ascent.
tips:
- Cue "knees out, chest proud" so the hips stay organized under the torso.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.

- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

name: Soccer Scrimmage
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Soccer Scrimmage.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.
tips:

name: Spin Class Interval
instructions:

2) Start easy for a few minutes, then bring cadence and resistance to the session target.

name: Stair Climber
instructions:
1) Set the machine for Stair Climber with a stable stance/seat and familiarize yourself with start/stop and resistance controls.
2) Begin easy for 2–3 minutes, then bring intensity to the target zone.
3) Keep posture tall, hands light on rails (unless the machine requires a grip), and movement smooth.
4) Breathe evenly. Cool down by lowering resistance before stepping off carefully.

- Step off only after the machine has slowed.
- Stop for dizziness, chest pain, or unusual joint pain.

name: Stair Walk
instructions:

2) Walk at the intended briskness, pushing through the big toe and letting the arms swing naturally opposite the legs.
3) Keep ribs stacked and avoid excessive forward hunch as fatigue rises.
4) Breathe through the nose and mouth as needed; finish by easing the pace for 2–3 minutes.

4) Ease out and switch sides.

name: Steady-State Row
instructions:
1) Strap feet securely for Steady-State Row, sit tall, and grab the handle with a relaxed grip.
2) Catch position: shins vertical-ish, arms long, shoulders in front of hips with a flat back.
3) Drive through the legs first, then open the hips, then draw the handle to the lower ribs. Reverse on the recovery: arms, hips, then knees.
4) Breathe out on the drive, in on the recovery. Keep strokes smooth rather than yanking with the arms.
tips:
- Legs do most of the work; arms finish.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Aim for a recovery that is longer than the drive on easy aerobic meters.

name: Step Up
instructions:
1) Start tall with the working implement, ribs stacked, and feet ready for the split stance used in Step Up.
2) Step or set into the lunge/split position with the front foot flat and the back heel lifted as the variation requires.
3) Lower with control until the back knee approaches the floor (or your comfortable depth) while the front knee tracks over the mid-toes.
4) Push through the front mid-foot to return. Keep the pelvis fairly level—avoid collapsing toward the working hip.

- Think "tall torso, quiet hips" rather than lunging with a floppy trunk.

- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorten the stride if the front heel lifts or the low back arches hard.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Slamming the back knee → control the last third of the descent.
- Leaning the chest onto the front thigh → brace and keep ribs over pelvis.
- Pushing mostly off the back foot when the variation should load the front leg → drive the front floor away.
safety_notes:
- Use support (wall/rail) until balance is reliable, especially on rear-foot elevated variations.
- Knee pain at the bottom usually means less depth or a shorter step.
- Keep landings soft on reverse/walking lunges—no crashing into the front heel.

name: Stiff Leg Deadlifts
instructions:
1) Set up for Stiff Leg Deadlifts with the working implement, feet hip-width, and a soft bend in the knees you can hold steady.
2) Brace the trunk, unlock the hips first, and push them rearward while the torso leans as one piece—imagine closing a car door with your hips.
3) Lower until you feel a strong hamstring load or reach the technique depth for this variation, keeping the bar/weight close to the legs if applicable.
4) Drive the floor away and bring hips forward to stand tall. Exhale as the hips finish under the shoulders.
tips:
- Soft knees stay fixed; the motion is hips back, not a deep squat.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Keep the load close to your center of mass—drifting away increases shear on the back.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Stiff Leg Deadlifts is a hip-hinge pattern that loads the posterior chain while the knees stay relatively soft, not deeply bent like a squat. Primary emphasis is on glutes and hamstrings. It teaches you to move from the hips with a neutral spine—useful for picking things up, sprint mechanics, and resilient back/hip strength. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Stiff Leg Deadlifts.
common_mistakes:
- Rounding the upper or lower back → shorten the range and re-brace before hinging.
- Squatting the hinge (knees slide forward too much) → push hips back and keep shins more vertical.
- Hyperextending at lockout → finish tall with glutes, not by dumping into the low back.
- Yanking the weight with the arms → let the hips create the power.
safety_notes:
- Avoid max loading if you cannot keep a long, braced spine through the whole set.
- Sharp shooting pain down a leg or into the spine is a stop signal—regress to a shorter hinge.
- Build hinge confidence with lighter loads and slower eccentrics before adding speed.

name: Straight Arm Pulldown
instructions:
1) Grip the working implement for Straight Arm Pulldown with shoulders set down away from the ears and a gentle hollow/brace through the trunk.
2) Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then drive elbows down toward the ribs/pockets.
3) Pull until the chin clears the bar or the handle reaches the target line for this variation, without shrugging into the neck.
4) Lower through a full, controlled reach. Exhale on the pull; keep legs quiet unless the variation uses a kip intentionally.
tips:
- Pack the shoulders before the first pull—start from structure, not a dead hang shrug.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use a band or foot assist before adding swing if you cannot control the eccentric.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Straight Arm Pulldown is a vertical pulling pattern that trains the lats and upper back to pull the body (or a load) along a high-to-low path. Primary emphasis is on back. It develops climbing strength, shoulder resilience, and torso control in a hang or overhead reach. Keep every rep of Straight Arm Pulldown looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Chin jutting to "cheat" height → pull the chest toward the bar and keep neck long.
- Half reps at the bottom → earn a full scapular reach each time.
- Excessive swinging → tighten the trunk and slow the lowering phase.
- Elbows flaring wildly → keep elbows tracking more under the wrists.
safety_notes:
- Elbow or shoulder pain on full hangs → shorten range or use an assisted variation.
- Dropping from the top without control overloads the elbows—own the eccentric.
- Warm up shoulders with lighter scap pulls before hard sets of Straight Arm Pulldown.

name: Sun Salutation A
instructions:
1) Arrive on a mat for Sun Salutation A, take a preparatory breath, and set a long spine.
2) Move into the pose piece by piece—feet/hands first, then hips/shoulders, then head gaze.
3) Soften where you can without collapsing the foundation; breathe steadily through the nose if comfortable.
4) Exit with control to a neutral position. Notice the after-effect rather than yanking out of the shape.
tips:
- Breath leads; depth follows.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Micro-bend joints if you tend to lock aggressively.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Sun Salutation A is a yoga-inspired mobility and control posture that links breath with a deliberate shape. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. The aim is a calm, sustainable position—not forcing end range for its own sake. Keep every rep of Sun Salutation A looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Forcing depth with breath held → back out and breathe.
- Collapsing into the shoulders/neck → press the floor away and keep neck long.
- Comparing your shape to photos → use sensation and stability as the guide.
- Bouncing in end range → stay still and breathe.
safety_notes:
- Sharp joint or spine pain means ease out immediately.
- Modify with blocks/bolsters rather than muscling into ranges you do not own.
- Avoid aggressive end-range stretching on cold tissues—warm up first.

name: Supine Hamstring Strap Stretch
instructions:
1) Set up for Supine Hamstring Strap Stretch with a long spine and the working leg positioned as the drill requires.
2) Hinge or extend until you feel a clear hamstring stretch—keep the back from excessively rounding just to go deeper.
3) Breathe and hold or oscillate gently in a tolerable range.
4) Ease out and switch sides.
tips:
- A soft knee often lets you feel hamstrings more than a locked, painful knee.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Pointing the toes up can bias different parts of the posterior chain—explore gently.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Supine Hamstring Strap Stretch targets hamstring length and tolerance to hip flexion with a relatively extended knee. Primary emphasis is on hamstrings. Useful before hinge work or after long sitting—without forcing a rounded back for extra inches. Focus on stacked ribs over pelvis throughout each rep of Supine Hamstring Strap Stretch.
common_mistakes:
- Rounding hard through the low back → shorten range and lengthen the spine.
- Yanking into deeper ranges → use breath and time under gentle tension.
- Ignoring neurological symptoms → back off if you get sharp shooting pain.
- Holding breath → slow exhales.
safety_notes:
- Sciatica-like symptoms mean stay gentle and consider professional guidance.
- Do not bounce aggressively into end range.
- Pair stretching with hinge strength so new range is usable.

name: Supine Twist
instructions:
1) Set a stable base for Supine Twist on a mat with an easy breath.
2) Initiate the spinal motion from the intended region (neck, mid-back, or low back as prescribed) rather than heaving from one stuck spot.
3) Move through a comfortable arc, matching breath to the motion (often exhale into flexion, inhale into extension—but comfort rules).
4) Return to neutral with control.
tips:
- Small, honest ranges beat dramatic collapsing shapes.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep hips relatively quiet unless the drill includes hip motion.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Supine Twist explores controlled spinal flexion, extension, or rotation to keep the trunk moving segment by segment. Primary emphasis is on back, with core assisting for control and finish. Move like you are oiling each vertebra—smooth and pain-free beats aggressive end-range forcing. Keep every rep of Supine Twist looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Dumping into one hinge point → distribute motion along the spine.
- Holding breath → keep air moving.
- Rushing rotations → move as if balancing a glass on the head.
- Forcing end range with arms → let the torso lead.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp spine pain, dizziness, or neurological symptoms.
- Disc-sensitive individuals may prefer smaller ranges and more support.
- Warm up before deep end-range twisting under load.

name: Swim Easy Laps
instructions:
1) Enter safely and take a few easy lengths or width crossings to feel the water for Swim Easy Laps.
2) Establish horizontal alignment—long spine, light core engagement, head in line with the spine.
3) Stroke with the intended pattern, rotating or kicking as the stroke requires, and breathe without lifting the head excessively.
4) Keep a sustainable pace; rest on the wall as needed. Exit carefully when finished.
tips:
- Relax the neck; gaze slightly downward in freestyle-type postures.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorter, smoother strokes usually beat thrashing when tired.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Swim Easy Laps is swim-based conditioning that combines breath control, horizontal posture, and coordinated limb propulsion. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. Swimming is joint-friendly cardio when technique stays relaxed and breathing is rhythmic. Keep every rep of Swim Easy Laps looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Holding breath too long → practice bilateral or comfortable rhythmic breathing.
- Crossing the midline with the hands → reach forward in the shoulder line.
- Kicking from bent knees only → initiate kick from the hips with soft knees.
- Tensing traps the whole set → exhale bubbles and soften the shoulders.
safety_notes:
- Swim in supervised areas appropriate to your skill level.
- Stop for dizziness, chest pain, or shoulder impingement that alters the stroke.
- Do not push hard sets without an easy warm-up in the water.

name: T-Bar Row
instructions:
1) Set your stance or seat for T-Bar Row with the working implement, arms long, and shoulders packed away from the ears.
2) Brace lightly, initiate by driving the elbows back, and pull the implement toward the ribcage/abdomen as the variation requires.
3) Squeeze the shoulder blades toward the back pockets at the end range without shrugging upward.
4) Return to a full reach with control—keep tension so the shoulders do not dump forward passively.
tips:
- Pull with the elbows, not by yanking the wrists.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Think "chest to the hands" on bodyweight rows; "hands to the ribs" on loaded rows.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: T-Bar Row is a horizontal pulling pattern that strengthens the upper back and scapular retractors while balancing pressing volume. Primary emphasis is on back. Strong rows improve posture under fatigue and help the shoulders tolerate pressing and daily reaching. Focus on mid-foot balance throughout each rep of T-Bar Row.
common_mistakes:
- Shrugging every rep → depress shoulders and lead with elbows.
- Using momentum from the hips/low back → pause briefly at full reach, then row.
- Cutting the range short → reach long without losing the brace, then pull fully.
- Craning the neck forward → keep eyes roughly forward and neck long.
safety_notes:
- Avoid yanking into end-range if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.
- Keep ribs from flaring on seated variations—brace first.
- Build volume gradually when returning from upper-back fatigue.

name: Tabata
instructions:
1) Warm up 3–5 minutes easy before Tabata so joints and breathing are ready.
2) Hit the work interval at a hard-but-repeatable intensity for the planned time or reps.
3) Use the rest interval to recover posture and breathing—walk, easy pedal, or complete rest as prescribed.
4) Repeat for the planned rounds. Cool down with easy movement and longer exhales.
tips:
- Leave one gear in reserve so the last interval still looks like the first.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Track work:rest so you can progress density thoughtfully next session.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Tabata is an interval-style conditioning bout that alternates harder efforts with recovery to raise cardiovascular fitness efficiently. It trains coordinated full-body effort rather than one isolated joint. The goal is repeatable quality across intervals—not a single heroic first round followed by collapse. Keep every rep of Tabata looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Sprinting round one then fading → pace to finish strong.
- Sloppy form under fatigue → regress the movement, not just the ego.
- Skipping warm-up → keep a short ramp even when short on time.
- Holding breath in work bouts → keep a forceful exhale rhythm.
safety_notes:
- If you feel chest pain, faintness, or disproportionate distress, stop and seek care as needed.
- Beginners should start with longer rests and fewer rounds.
- Pair HIIT with easier days; daily max intervals raise injury and burnout risk.

name: Technique Row
instructions:
1) Strap feet securely for Technique Row, sit tall, and grab the handle with a relaxed grip.
2) Catch position: shins vertical-ish, arms long, shoulders in front of hips with a flat back.
3) Drive through the legs first, then open the hips, then draw the handle to the lower ribs. Reverse on the recovery: arms, hips, then knees.
4) Breathe out on the drive, in on the recovery. Keep strokes smooth rather than yanking with the arms.
tips:
- Legs do most of the work; arms finish.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Aim for a recovery that is longer than the drive on easy aerobic meters.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Technique Row is a full-body cardio pull that sequences legs–hips–trunk–arms on a rower or similar erg. Primary emphasis is on back and legs, with core and arms assisting for control and finish. Done well, it trains aerobic power without impact while reinforcing a strong hinge and posture. Keep every rep of Technique Row looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Early arm pull → keep arms long until legs nearly finish.
- Rounding at the catch → hinge with a braced flat back.
- Shooting the seat (legs only, then yank) → connect legs and hips as one drive.
- Over-leaning at the finish → lean slightly, then recover immediately.
safety_notes:
- Lower intensity if you feel sharp low-back pain at the catch.
- Build volume gradually—rowers can spike heart rate quickly.
- Keep the chain/path clear and feet strapped.

name: Tempo Run
instructions:
1) Start Tempo Run with an easy walk or light jog to raise temperature and wake up calves/hips.
2) Settle into the target pace with a tall posture, soft forward lean from the ankles, and quick, light foot contacts under the hips.
3) Keep cadence relatively quick; avoid overstriding that heels slam far in front of the body.
4) Breathe rhythmically (for example, a comfortable 2–2 or 3–3 pattern). Finish with a walk to cool down.
tips:
- Easy days should feel conversational unless the session is explicitly a hard interval.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorten stride and increase cadence if you hear loud heel slamming.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Tempo Run is a running-based cardio bout focused on sustainable gait mechanics and aerobic (or mixed) conditioning. Easy-to-moderate running builds work capacity; faster variations train speed and anaerobic power when recovered well. Treat Tempo Run as practice for positions you want under fatigue—not just a checkbox set.
common_mistakes:
- Overstriding → land closer under the hips.
- Hunched chest / crossed arms → open the chest and swing arms forward-back.
- Starting too fast → first minutes easier than ego wants.
- Holding breath on hills → exhale deliberately on the effort.
safety_notes:
- Increase weekly running volume gradually; sudden spikes raise injury risk.
- Sharp shin, knee, or Achilles pain is a stop/regress signal—walk or cross-train.
- Use footwear that feels stable for your gait and surface.

name: Tennis Rally
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Tennis Rally.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.
tips:
- Quality footwork and soft landings matter as much as scoreboard intensity.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Drink water between bouts in long pickup games.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

Keep every rep of Tennis Rally looking like the demo rep you would coach a friend through.
common_mistakes:
- Going max intensity with cold tissues → warm up first.
- Planting awkwardly on tired legs → shorten sessions when form gets reckless.
- Ignoring rest in continuous games → schedule drink/rest breaks.
- Holding rigid breath under pressure → reset with an exhale between plays.
safety_notes:
- Use appropriate footwear and clear playing space.
- Stop for acute joint injuries; do not "run off" sharp pain.
- Match competitive intensity to your current conditioning and skill.

name: Thoracic Opener
instructions:
1) Set a stable spine for Thoracic Opener on a mat, lightly braced so the ribs stay down.
2) Explore the shoulder/T-spine path with smooth arcs or holds as prescribed.
3) Breathe through the end range without shrugging into the ears.
4) Reverse carefully and compare sides.
tips:
- Think "long neck, heavy shoulder blades" during stretches.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- If you only feel the front of the shoulder pinching, reduce range and adjust angle.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

- Shrugging to force range → depress shoulders and move slower.
- Turning a shoulder drill into a low-back stretch → keep pelvis quiet.
- Bouncing into end range → use controlled holds.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp impingement or numbness/tingling down the arm.
- Post-dislocation or post-op shoulders: stay inside approved ranges.
- Warm up before aggressive end-range band work.

name: Tibialis Raise Stretch
instructions:
1) Set your foot position for Tibialis Raise Stretch with the heel down when the drill requires it.
2) Move the knee or foot through the prescribed arc slowly, keeping pressure distributed through the foot.
3) Pause in the challenging but non-painful end range and breathe.
4) Return and repeat, matching effort on both sides.
tips:
- Drive the knee toward the little-toe side for many dorsiflexion drills to free the ankle.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the heel heavy when the drill calls for it—cheating the heel up skips the point.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Tibialis Raise Stretch improves ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion control so the knee can travel more freely in squats and lunges. Primary emphasis is on calves. Small daily doses often beat rare aggressive stretching. Focus on full usable range throughout each rep of Tibialis Raise Stretch.
common_mistakes:
- Pronating hard to fake range → guide the knee more over mid-toes/little toe as coached.
- Bouncing aggressively → use slow oscillations or static holds.
- Ignoring the stiffer side → start sets there.
- Holding breath → exhale into the end range.
safety_notes:
- Sharp Achilles or joint-line pain means stop and regress.
- Recent ankle sprains need gradual, controlled range—not forced stretches.
- Pair mobility with strength in the new range (e.g., heel-elevated squats) when appropriate.

description: Trap Bar Deadlift is a hip-hinge pattern that loads the posterior chain while the knees stay relatively soft, not deeply bent like a squat. Primary emphasis is on back. common_mistakes:
- Rounding the upper or lower back → shorten the range and re-brace before hinging.
- Squatting the hinge (knees slide forward too much) → push hips back and keep shins more vertical.
- Hyperextending at lockout → finish tall with glutes, not by dumping into the low back.
- Yanking the weight with the arms → let the hips create the power.
safety_notes:
- Avoid max loading if you cannot keep a long, braced spine through the whole set.
- Sharp shooting pain down a leg or into the spine is a stop signal—regress to a shorter hinge.
- Build hinge confidence with lighter loads and slower eccentrics before adding speed.

name: Treadmill Incline Interval
instructions:
1) Start Treadmill Incline Interval with an easy walk or light jog to raise temperature and wake up calves/hips.
2) Settle into the target pace with a tall posture, soft forward lean from the ankles, and quick, light foot contacts under the hips.
3) Keep cadence relatively quick; avoid overstriding that heels slam far in front of the body.
4) Breathe rhythmically (for example, a comfortable 2–2 or 3–3 pattern). Finish with a walk to cool down.
tips:
- Easy days should feel conversational unless the session is explicitly a hard interval.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Shorten stride and increase cadence if you hear loud heel slamming.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.
description: Treadmill Incline Interval is a running-based cardio bout focused on sustainable gait mechanics and aerobic (or mixed) conditioning. - Overstriding → land closer under the hips.
- Hunched chest / crossed arms → open the chest and swing arms forward-back.
- Starting too fast → first minutes easier than ego wants.
- Holding breath on hills → exhale deliberately on the effort.
safety_notes:
- Increase weekly running volume gradually; sudden spikes raise injury risk.
- Sharp shin, knee, or Achilles pain is a stop/regress signal—walk or cross-train.
- Use footwear that feels stable for your gait and surface.

name: Tree Pose
instructions:

2) Move into the pose piece by piece—feet/hands first, then hips/shoulders, then head gaze.
3) Soften where you can without collapsing the foundation; breathe steadily through the nose if comfortable.
4) Exit with control to a neutral position. Notice the after-effect rather than yanking out of the shape.
tips:
- Breath leads; depth follows.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Micro-bend joints if you tend to lock aggressively.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

safety_notes:
- Sharp joint or spine pain means ease out immediately.
- Modify with blocks/bolsters rather than muscling into ranges you do not own.
- Avoid aggressive end-range stretching on cold tissues—warm up first.

name: Triceps Kickback
instructions:
1) Set a stable posture for Triceps Kickback with the working implement, isolating the intended joint while the rest of the body stays quiet.
2) Move through the target range with a smooth tempo—no snapping out of the bottom.
3) Pause briefly where the muscle is most challenged if it helps you feel the right tissue working.
4) Return under control to the start position and reset brace/posture before the next rep.
tips:
- Smaller muscles win with crisp control, not ego load.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- If other muscles take over, reduce load until the target tissue leads.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

common_mistakes:
- Swinging the weight → shorten range and slow the eccentric.

- Rushing the stretch position → own the lengthened end without pain.

safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp joint pain; mild muscle burn is expected, pinching is not.
- Keep wrists neutral on curl/extension patterns when possible.
- Pair isolation work with compounds rather than replacing foundational patterns entirely.

name: Tuck Jump
instructions:
1) Set an athletic stance for Tuck Jump with your bodyweight if used, weight on mid-foot, and eyes forward.
2) Load the hips and knees quickly (or step into the jump as prescribed), then extend through hips, knees, and ankles to leave the ground.
3) Land softly on the mid-foot with knees tracking over toes and hips absorbing like springs.
4) Reset between reps if quality drops. Breathe out on the effort of the jump.
tips:
- Quiet landings beat maximal height when learning.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Use arms deliberately; floppy arms waste power.

name: Upright Row
instructions:
1) Set your stance or seat for Upright Row with the working implement, arms long, and shoulders packed away from the ears.
2) Brace lightly, initiate by driving the elbows back, and pull the implement toward the ribcage/abdomen as the variation requires.
3) Squeeze the shoulder blades toward the back pockets at the end range without shrugging upward.
4) Return to a full reach with control—keep tension so the shoulders do not dump forward passively.
tips:
- Pull with the elbows, not by yanking the wrists.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.

- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Avoid yanking into end-range if you feel pinching in the front of the shoulder.

name: Volleyball Game
instructions:
1) Warm up with light movement and a few rehearsal reps of the key actions in Volleyball Game.
2) Play or drill at an intensity that matches the session goal (skills, conditioning, or both).
3) Keep posture athletic—hips ready, feet active, eyes up—especially when fatigued.
4) Rotate roles/rest as needed. Cool down with easy movement and mobility for the heavily used joints.

instructions:

2) Walk at the intended briskness, pushing through the big toe and letting the arms swing naturally opposite the legs.
3) Keep ribs stacked and avoid excessive forward hunch as fatigue rises.
4) Breathe through the nose and mouth as needed; finish by easing the pace for 2–3 minutes.

- Brisk usually means you can talk in sentences but not sing easily.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.

- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

name: Wall Angel
instructions:

2) Explore the shoulder/T-spine path with smooth arcs or holds as prescribed.
3) Breathe through the end range without shrugging into the ears.
4) Reverse carefully and compare sides.

- Think "long neck, heavy shoulder blades" during stretches.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- If you only feel the front of the shoulder pinching, reduce range and adjust angle.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.
description: Wall Angel restores usable motion through the shoulders, thoracic spine, or chest so overhead and pressing postures feel less cramped. common_mistakes:
- Flaring ribs to reach overhead → re-stack and shorten the reach.
- Shrugging to force range → depress shoulders and move slower.
- Turning a shoulder drill into a low-back stretch → keep pelvis quiet.
- Bouncing into end range → use controlled holds.
safety_notes:
- Stop for sharp impingement or numbness/tingling down the arm.
- Post-dislocation or post-op shoulders: stay inside approved ranges.
- Warm up before aggressive end-range band work.

name: Wall Ankle Mobilization
instructions:
1) Set your foot position for Wall Ankle Mobilization with the heel down when the drill requires it.
2) Move the knee or foot through the prescribed arc slowly, keeping pressure distributed through the foot.
3) Pause in the challenging but non-painful end range and breathe.
4) Return and repeat, matching effort on both sides.
tips:
- Drive the knee toward the little-toe side for many dorsiflexion drills to free the ankle.
- Shorten the range or use support until the pattern feels stable.
- Add a small pause in the hardest position before increasing load or volume.
- Keep the heel heavy when the drill calls for it—cheating the heel up skips the point.
- Start light and prioritize clean positions over speed or load.

- Bouncing aggressively → use slow oscillations or static holds.
- Ignoring the stiffer side → start sets there.
- Holding breath → exhale into the end range.
safety_notes:
- Sharp Achilles or joint-line pain means stop and regress.
- Recent ankle sprains need gradual, controlled range—not forced stretches.
- Pair mobility with strength in the new range (e.g., heel-elevated squats) when appropriate.

name: Wall Sit
instructions:

2) Brace as if preparing for a light poke to the stomach—enough tension to keep the torso quiet.
3) Perform the movement (hold, reach, lift, or roll) without letting the low back dump into extension or collapse into a hard crunch unless the variation is a flexion drill.
4) Breathe steadily; do not hold a panicked breath for the entire set. Finish by releasing tension with control.

- Quality bracing beats frantic flopping for "more reps."

- If the low back takes over, shorten the lever (bend knees, reduce reach) immediately.
- Use a challenge you can repeat with the same quality on the last rep as the first.

- Stop for sharp spine pain or neurological symptoms.
- Build duration and range gradually; core tissue tolerates progressive loading best.

name: Wide Grip Lat Pulldown
instructions:

2) Initiate by depressing the shoulder blades, then drive elbows down toward the ribs/pockets.
3) Pull until the chin clears the bar or the handle reaches the target line for this variation, without shrugging into the neck.

2) Lower with control as the shoulder blades stay gently retracted/depressed; stop at a depth you can reverse without the shoulders dumping forward.
3) Press back to the start by driving through the palms/chest, keeping ribs down and neck neutral.
4) Exhale near the sticking point of the press; keep elbows from flaring into a hard 90° "T" unless the variation specifically requires it.
tips:
- Stack wrists over elbows at the bottom for a stronger press path.
- Reduce range, support, or load when positions start to drift.
- Progress by improving range quality first, then load or density.
- Leave a little tension in the mid-back so the shoulders have a stable shelf.

- Comparing your shape to photos → use sensation and stability as the guide.
- Bouncing in end range → stay still and breathe.
safety_notes:
- Sharp joint or spine pain means ease out immediately.
- Modify with blocks/bolsters rather than muscling into ranges you do not own.
- Avoid aggressive end-range stretching on cold tissues—warm up first.
